#5058. Britain to spend £4 billion on grid bottlenecks. Can Bitcoin use the wasted wind?

Flexible mines could use curtailed Scottish wind, but most recent constraint spending paid for replacement power elsewhere. A proposed demand service would start in 2028.

Britain’s grid operator forecasts about £4 billion in costs from transmission bottlenecks in 2027, putting a practical question to Bitcoin mining’s flexible-power pitch: can miners cut costs by using Scottish wind that cannot reach other consumers?

The National Energy System Operator (NESO) published the forecast on Nov. 12. Its latest cost breakdown shows why the answer depends on where a mine connects and which expense it actually avoids.

Thermal constraints arise when transmission lines cannot safely carry all the available electricity. NESO can then pay generators to reduce output while securing replacement supply elsewhere.

The forecast concerns thermal constraints, rather than all electricity balancing costs. It is sensitive to gas prices and network availability. NESO estimates costs would be 16% lower without network outages, although those outages also enable reinforcement intended to ease future bottlenecks.

In its Nov. 9 outturn explanation, NESO reported total balancing costs of about £3 billion for 2025/26, including roughly £2 billion for thermal constraints. A little under £500 million was paid to wind farms to turn down.

Around 75% of thermal constraint costs paid for replacement energy, predominantly from gas units.

Scotland nevertheless presents a potential use case. NESO says 28% of wind in the northern area above a transmission boundary known as B6 was curtailed in 2025/26, compared with 13% across Great Britain.

A flexible mine could reduce wind turn-down costs by consuming otherwise curtailed electricity at a connection and time that helps manage the relevant bottleneck. But adding northern demand does not itself deliver more power south. While the boundary remains binding and southern demand is unchanged, replacement supply remains necessary there.

That limits the savings claim: reduced wind turn-down does not establish an equivalent reduction in gas generation, consumer bills or emissions.

NESO forecasts £3.9 billion in thermal constraint costs for 2027. Using curtailed wind tackles only part of the problem.

Illustration: wind is curtailed behind a binding boundary; replacement supply still serves unchanged southern demand.

Illustration: mining uses some surplus behind a binding boundary; replacement supply still serves unchanged southern demand.

A local mine may reduce wind turn-down costs while replacement supply is still needed beyond the bottleneck.

The 2025/26 share is not a 2027 breakdown. Mining state is conditional on suitable connection, timing and dispatch. No Bitcoin-specific approval, payment entitlement, gas saving or consumer benefit is established.

The share strip represents NESO’s approximate 75% replacement-energy share for 2025/26. State diagrams are qualitative illustrations of a binding boundary with unchanged southern demand, not observed UK mining operations. No savings or generation volumes are calculated.

The 2025/26 share is not a 2027 breakdown. Mining state is conditional on suitable connection, timing and dispatch. No Bitcoin-specific approval, payment entitlement, gas saving or consumer benefit is established.

The Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance’s mining survey offers evidence that miners can adjust consumption. Respondents reported curtailing 888 GWh of electrical load during 2023. That measures demand turned down, while absorbing surplus Scottish wind would require demand to turn up at the right location and time.

The survey covered 49 firms representing 48% of Bitcoin’s network hashrate at collection, with activity concentrated in North America. It does not establish profitable intermittent mining in Britain. Electricity accounted for more than 80% of surveyed miners’ cash-based operating expenses.

NESO’s November thermal constraints report identifies additional flexible demand in constrained areas as a mitigation. Its March 5 proposed Demand for Constraints design focused on Scottish boundaries. It contemplated registration and dispatch through the Balancing Mechanism, NESO’s system for directing electricity supply and demand in real time, with routes for both new connections and existing assets creating additional flexible demand. The March design proposed service deliveries from 2028, after the year covered by the forecast. It did not establish a Bitcoin-specific approval or payment entitlement.

For a mine, a usable connection, service qualification and enough operating hours to cover costs would all matter. For consumers, the relevant comparison is the expense actually avoided after accounting for the costs the project adds.

NESO’s test is overall system cost. The roughly £4 billion forecast identifies the scale of a grid problem; it does not price a mining solution.

#5057. Bitcoin Price Briefly Crashes to $67,500, Lowest Since August, as Dollar Holds 19-Month High

Bitcoin price traded near $69,800 on Friday morning after briefly crashing to about $67,555 around midnight Eastern, its lowest level since mid-August, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data. The rebound held after October producer prices rose less than economists had expected, though the U.S. dollar remained near a 19-month high and traders still fully priced a December Federal Reserve rate hike.

Bitcoin price was trading near $72,800 at this time Thursday. It slipped toward $71,000 by Thursday evening, then gave way late at night, breaking below $70,000 and sliding to that midnight low. The move also pushed the bitcoin price below its 200-week moving average, a long-term trend line near $68,000. Buyers lifted it back above $69,000 before sunrise, and the rebound extended toward $69,800 after the producer-price report.

The U.S. Dollar Index held above 103 Friday after a three-day rally took it to its highest level since April 2025. The 10-year Treasury yield was near 5.15% ahead of the data, and two-year yields, which track Fed expectations most closely, were on pace for their worst week since 2024, Bloomberg reported.

Traders still see an 88% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting and a 12% chance of a half-point move, CME FedWatch data show. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has added a 50-basis-point increase to the discussion, and New York Fed President John Williams said Thursday that inflation remains high and policymakers need to take further action.

Higher rates raise the cost of holding an asset that pays no interest, and a stronger dollar tends to drain demand for risk assets. Both have pressured the bitcoin price since this week’s hotter-than-expected consumer price index.

Bitcoin has also broken from tech stocks. It fell 5.9% between Nov. 5 and Nov. 12 while the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.4%, a sign it is trading more on yields and the dollar than on the AI trade. Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 0.6% Friday after the producer-price report, as investors also weighed Nvidia’s announcement that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO.

The break below $70,000 set off a wave of forced selling. About $1.64 billion in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, with bets on higher prices making up nearly 89% of the total and bitcoin positions accounting for $916 million.

U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs added to the pressure. The funds posted about $47.7 million in net outflows Thursday, their sixth straight day of withdrawals, bringing the run to roughly $1.49 billion. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) alone bled about $2 billion over nine sessions through Wednesday, and the group has now flipped to about $1.56 billion in net outflows for 2026.

Sentiment has soured with it. A widely watched crypto fear and greed gauge dropped to 20 Friday, its lowest reading since July 8, and bitcoin is now on track for a second straight down year.

Positioning has turned defensive. Average perpetual futures funding rates turned negative for the first time in a month as the price fell toward $68,500, meaning short sellers are now paying to hold their bets. Order books are also thin. Bitcoin order-book depth across major exchanges fell to $72 million on Nov. 9, roughly 33% below normal levels. “Liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction,” said Tanay Ved, a senior research associate at Talos.

The Labor Department said Friday that the Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% in October, short of the 0.4% monthly increase economists had expected, after a revised 1.4% advance in September. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, increased 0.3%, matching forecasts. On an unadjusted basis, the headline index was up 6.5% from a year earlier, the largest 12-month rise since November 2022. The slightly cooler report took some pressure off the dollar, which still held above 103, but a December rate hike remains fully priced, leaving limited relief for the bitcoin price heading into the weekend.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $69,800.

#5056. Morning Minute: Tokenized Stock Venues Are Launching Without Big Tech’s Approval

Morning Minute: Tokenized Stock Venues Are Launching Without Big Tech’s Approval

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🏛️ OKX’s Tokenized Stock Venue Launches Without Big Tech

In September, after the CLARITY Act died in the Senate, the SEC created an innovation exemption letting venues trade tokenized versions of US stocks without waiting for new legislation. It came with one condition. A company that doesn’t want a third party minting tokens of its shares can object in writing within 30 days, and that’s the end of it.

Companies have been objecting ever since. The count at the OKXICE venue went from 22 in October to 50, then 56, and as of its November 5 notice, 67. Every member of the Magnificent Seven is on that list.

OKXICE is launching anyway, on November 23. The venue will list more than 70 assets, though 59 of them are Direxion ETFs. The individual stocks that made it through are Coinbase, Circle, Robinhood, Strategy, BitGo, Securitize and Better.com. Strategy is also tokenizing its preferred shares.

Securitize handles the tokenization, each token is backed one-for-one by a real share and carries dividends and voting rights, and trading runs through Uniswap v4 pools on X Layer, OKX’s Ethereum layer-2.

So a venture between a global exchange and the parent of the New York Stock Exchange built a tokenized equities market, and what it opens with is seven crypto companies and a series of leveraged ETFs.

Notably, this news comes just a day after the NYSE picked Avalanche to handle clearing and settlement for its own 24/7 tokenized securities platform, with a fourth-quarter target for launch after about a year of testing. The NYSE has signed agreements with Broadridge, Computershare, Equiniti and Superstate to support issuer-sponsored tokenized securities and transfer-agent functions. When the company’s own share registry issues the token, there is nothing to veto.

DTCC is doing a version of this too, with a tokenization service that went live October 28 on the Canton Network carrying 20 participants including Bank of America, Citi, JPMorgan and Citadel Securities. Morgan Stanley has already run equities and Treasuries through it.

Progress is being made, slowly but surely. It just gets built slowly, through transfer agents and clearing houses, by the incumbents. Now we wait to see how the market reacts to these first launches…

Pickleball shoes need to provide support, so buying the lightest shoe possible is not the smartest move. You can also consider tennis shoes and cross-trainers due to their similar support-first construction. Avoid featherlight running shoes that are built for a different type of movement.

Mesh is the most common and best material to look for in the upper of a pickleball shoe. However, like weight, you don't necessarily need the most breathable mesh possible. When looking at the midsole, aim for a shoe that has supportive cushioning (like EVA foam) and keeps a relatively low profile. I also partnered with our other writers and editors at Men's Health to help select the best pickleball shoes we’ve tested in the past few years, available. We’ve compiled a guide to the best all-day play, taking great note of each shoe's stability, durability, weight, and price point. Special consideration was taken into account for pickleball shoes that had excellent traction and stability since those two qualities are the most important in a pickleball shoe.

There is a lot of crossover from effective tennis shoes to pickleball shoes. So we also spoke to experts like Life Time Galleria Tennis Leader Gary Armstrong (who has been playing tennis for 36 years and has been an instructor for 17 years) and Life Time Charlotte Tennis Leader Eric Winn (who has been a tennis coach for 24 years and still plays in the 5.0 USTA leagues) to get their takes on the best tennis shoes for men. With minimal differences, some of their picks made it to this guide.

If you're someone who's going to play pickleball once or twice for recreation, then you could get away with a low-profile running shoe. But if you're expecting to play any more than that, we strongly recommend buying a proper pair of pickleball shoes.

The reason we don't recommend wearing just any type of running shoe is that running shoes are made for forward motion, so there's often less emphasis on reinforcing the shoe for side-to-side movements. Running shoes also have less structure and stability than what you want in a pickleball shoe, as the running styles these days are made to be as lightweight and breathable as possible (with high cushioned stacks), which means less focus on overall support.

So, to be clear, you should steer from wearing running shoes for pickleball if you expect to play the game on a regular basis. A proper pickleball shoe is a smart investment that will help give you traction and stability while greatly decreasing the chance of rolling an ankle or spraining a knee.

#5053. Robots now run AI-written code without an AI calling the shots, succeeding 92% of the time

Robots completed 221 of 240 trials using Claude-written programs for tasks such as uncapping bottles. Human help was available during development, not execution.

Robot programs developed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 coding agent completed 221 of 240 physical evaluation trials, ACE-CaP-0 researchers reported in a study posted November 12. The result shows that task-specific skills can persist in code and run without the coding agent choosing each action.

The researchers behind ACE-CaP-0, a method for developing robot control programs, reported a 92.1% success rate across eight tasks. Each program was frozen before 30 separate evaluation trials, with no further updates. Human guidance and demonstrations were available during development.

The experiment separates program development from repeated execution. The agent's work produced a program that could be used repeatedly. During evaluation, that program still used perception and control systems to respond to observations, while its decision rules stayed fixed. Neither a human nor the coding agent remained in the execution loop.

ACE-CaP-0 separates assisted program development from repeated execution with live perception and control.

Human assistance is available during development; the frozen task program runs without a human or coding agent in the execution loop.

Authors' preprint account. Development permits human assistance; demonstration-collection resets are excluded from the ten-reset budget. Repeated execution on tested tasks does not establish reuse under new conditions.

Source-bound qualitative process diagram from sections 2 to 4. Arrows show code revision and runtime sensing relationships, not timing, trial quantities or comparative efficiency.

Authors' preprint account. Development permits human assistance; demonstration-collection resets are excluded from the ten-reset budget. Repeated execution on tested tasks does not establish reuse under new conditions.

Author-reported successful trials out of 30 for each frozen program. These were physical evaluation trials, separate from development; Table 1, November 12 preprint.

The physical setup used two Agilex PIPERX arms and three cameras. Tasks included inserting a charger, uncapping a bottle and packing shoes. Charger insertion succeeded in all 30 trials; bread packing, the weakest result, succeeded in 25. Mean physical execution times across tasks ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes.

During development, the coding agent wrote, ran, inspected and revised its code using physical feedback. It could ask for textual advice or demonstrations in which a person physically guided the robot arms. Those demonstrations supplied video, arm trajectories and key joint poses.

Development allowed at most ten human-assisted scene resets per task. Resets used to collect demonstrations were excluded, and the budget counted scene resets rather than all robot executions or demonstrations.

The agent could also use simulated experiments when they helped resolve a development question. In a charger-insertion comparison, on-demand simulation produced a program with 100% evaluation success, versus 86.7% for development without simulation. The comparison used one development run per condition.

That comparison also illustrates a cost trade-off. Development took 2.6 hours with on-demand simulation versus 3.7 hours without it, while output-token usage increased from 730,000 to 1,090,000. The time and token figures leave total development costs unresolved; the researchers call for accounting that includes demonstration effort.

Repeating evaluation trials measures how the resulting program performs. Establishing how consistently the development process produces an equally capable program requires separate development runs across tasks.

ACE-CaP-0 leaves behind task-specific programs that can execute repeatedly with fresh observations and fixed decision rules. The study provides evidence for that form of skill reuse after human-assisted development. Testing those routines under new conditions is the next step toward establishing how broadly they can be reused.

#5052. President Trump Taps Two Democrats in Bipartisan Slate of SEC and CFTC Nominees as Both Agencies Run Short-Handed

President Donald Trump sent the Senate four nominees for the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission on Thursday, his first picks for either agency in about a year and the first Democrats he has put forward for them.

Former CFTC Commissioner Kristin Johnson, a Democrat, and Republican Steven Levine were nominated to the SEC. Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland were nominated to the CFTC, Bloomberg Law reported.

Each nominee needs Senate confirmation. The Senate Banking Committee will handle the SEC picks, while the Senate Agriculture Committee will take up the CFTC pair before any vote by the full chamber.

Levine was tapped for the SEC seat left by Hester Peirce, whose term expired, for a term running through June 5, 2030. He most recently served as general counsel and a senior adviser at the White House Council of Economic Advisers and previously worked at the SEC as counsel and deputy chief of staff to Commissioner Mark Uyeda.

Peirce led the SEC’s Crypto Task Force and was one of the agency’s most vocal supporters of clearer crypto rules.

Johnson would take the seat formerly held by Democrat Caroline Crenshaw, for a term ending June 5, 2029. She served as a CFTC commissioner until 2025 and is a former law school professor. During her time at the CFTC, she spoke often about digital assets, including custody and decentralized finance.

Both CFTC nominees come from the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the derivatives regulator. Anonick is legislative counsel to Chairman John Boozman and was a lead negotiator on the committee’s portion of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. He was nominated to the seat once held by former Chairman Rostin Behnam, for a term ending June 19, 2031.

Rowland is a CFTC attorney detailed to the committee who also worked on the Clarity Act and the committee’s 2024 crypto bill. He previously served on Johnson’s staff at the CFTC, according to his LinkedIn profile. He would fill the remainder of former Commissioner Summer Mersinger’s term, which expires April 13, 2028.

Both agencies can seat up to five commissioners, with no more than three from one party. The SEC currently has two, Chairman Paul Atkins and Commissioner Mark Uyeda. Chairman Mike Selig is the CFTC’s only sitting commissioner.

The timing puts the nominees in front of a Senate in its lame-duck session, weeks after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, one of crypto’s sharpest critics, is expected to chair the Banking Committee when the new Congress is seated in January.

The pairing of Democrats with Republicans could matter for confirmation. After the election, TD Cowen’s Jaret Seiberg told clients he did not expect Democrats to confirm Trump nominees unless the president filled Democratic seats at agencies such as the SEC, a step he called unlikely. Thursday’s slate does exactly that at both regulators.

The nominations also land with crypto market structure legislation stalled. The Clarity Act failed a Senate cloture vote 49-50 on Sept. 15 and dies on Jan. 3 unless the lame-duck session revives it.

Without new law, the SEC and CFTC have set crypto policy largely on their own this year. Selig’s CFTC opened the door to equity perpetual futures, and a federal judge later said the agency likely overstepped while letting trading continue.

The White House did not say when it expects the Senate to act. The open question is whether a Senate heading for Democratic control moves the four nominees before January, or leaves the SEC and CFTC running with skeleton commissions into 2027.

#5051. Bitcoin now looks cheap by one measure after $1 billion in ETF outflows

Bitcoin’s valuation signal looks cheaper, but five completed ETF sessions lost $1 billion. A durable recovery still needs buyers.

Bitcoin's latest on-chain valuation alert has arrived after five consecutive sessions of net redemptions from US spot exchange-traded funds, highlighting a lower valuation before the demand evidence confirms that buyers are absorbing supply.

CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost reported on Nov. 15 that Bitcoin's market-value-to-realized-value ratio, or MVRV, had fallen below 1.2. The ratio compares Bitcoin's market value with the value of coins at their last-moved prices. He called it the third trigger of his valuation preset during the 2026 bear market. Yet five completed ETF sessions through Nov. 13 recorded combined net outflows of $1 billion, according to Farside Investors.

The alert identifies a gap between lower valuation and returning demand. A lower aggregate valuation does not show whether new buying can absorb coins being moved at a loss.

CryptoSlate’s Bitcoin page showed $65,461 in a snapshot captured at 10:44 UTC on Nov. 15. The page said its price had refreshed about five minutes earlier.

MVRV divides market capitalization by realized capitalization, which values coins at the prices when they last moved. It compares today's aggregate market value with an on-chain cost proxy.

Darkfost identified earlier alerts in February, when Bitcoin had crossed $60,000, and June to July, when it reached $57,000. He also said the preset is adjusted over time to reflect MVRV's long-term decline.

That adjustment matters to the historical comparison. The post does not supply a threshold-change history or reproducible backtest showing what followed each signal. Three alerts within a bear market do not establish three durable bottoms.

CryptoQuant's methodology guide discusses MVRV below 1 as a possible-bottom region. That is distinct from Darkfost's adjusted sub-1.2 alert.

Unlike the specific holder-cost cluster examined in CryptoSlate's Nov. 14 coverage, MVRV covers Bitcoin's aggregate valuation. Both use last-movement information, which records historical positioning rather than current buying.

A separate CryptoQuant note from XWIN Japan, available on Nov. 15, cited a spent output profit ratio, or SOPR, near 0.98. The note did not identify the variant or exact observation time, limiting comparisons with other SOPR readings.

SOPR compares the aggregate dollar value of spent outputs when they move with their value when created. Below 1 means the measured outputs moved at an aggregate loss. It does not establish that every transfer was an exchange sale.

Adjusted SOPR excludes outputs younger than one hour, while long- and short-term-holder versions separate older and newer coins around a 155-day boundary. Those series need to remain distinct when assessing whether loss realization is easing.

Demand offers a separate test. Farside Investors recorded $185 million in net outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs on Nov. 13. That capped five consecutive sessions of net withdrawals from Nov. 9 through Nov. 13.

These are dated fund flows, not Sunday transactions, and ETFs represent only one channel of Bitcoin demand. Still, continuing redemptions leave that channel withdrawing capital rather than supplying the recurring inflows that would strengthen a recovery case.

As our beauty editor, I’m often asked by my friends about LED face masks. Do they actually work? The short answer is yes, but there are some caveats. Even the best LED face masks won’t do much if they’re collecting dust in the back of my closet. I actually need to be committed to using my new device regularly. I see the best results when I use my CurrentBody Skin 2 Face Mask for 10 minutes, three times a week. When I stop for several months, I notice my complexion is duller and hyperpigmentation from acne is slower to fade.

The minor trade-off of temporarily looking like I haunt the Paris Opera House is worth it because my results speak for themselves. I’ve been using mine consistently for eight years, and my face is noticeably clearer, even-toned, and radiant.

LED face masks are usually class II devices. They’re either FDA-listed or FDA-registered, meaning the brand notified the agency about the device. However, this listing doesn’t indicate the products are approved, cleared, or authorized by the agency.

They could also be FDA-cleared, meaning they are similar to other devices that are legally marketed for the same use. Our editors prioritized testing face masks that are either FDA-listed, -registered, or -cleared. And I referenced the FDA database to verify the status of our recommendations.

Yes, it’s generally low-risk for most users, says dermatologist Dendy Engelman, MD. "LED light therapy is not an invasive treatment, and when done properly, the risks are minimal," she says. #5049. DTCC to Bring Tokenized Stocks and Treasuries to Solana in 2027

DTCC to Bring Tokenized Stocks and Treasuries to Solana in 2027

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the backbone of U.S. securities settlement, plans to bring its tokenized securities to Solana, it announced on Thursday.

The firm will connect the DTCC Tokenization Service (DTS) to the Solana network, allowing eligible assets held by its Depository Trust Company (DTC) subsidiary to be converted into tokens on Solana. The integration is planned for the second half of 2027.

BREAKING: @The_DTCC to tokenize custodied assets on Solana. announced plans to connect the DTCC Tokenization Service to Solana, enabling the tokenization of eligible DTC-custodied assets on the network.

The integration is planned for the second half of 2027, further advancing… pic.twitter.com/gXszWFgUOX

"DTCC is bringing regulated, DTC-tokenized securities to another major blockchain ecosystem, giving market participants greater choice in where they access and utilize tokenized assets," DTCC CEO Frank La Salla said.

DTS went live on October 28 on the Canton Network and DTCC's own private blockchain, built on the Besu framework, with more networks due to be added in 2027, according to DTCC's launch announcement. The service creates tokenized "digital twins" of securities held at DTC, which custodies more than $114 trillion in assets. Solana joins Stellar and Circle's Arc blockchain, which are expected to be added in 2027, according to a DTCC fact sheet.

Under a no-action letter from the SEC, the service is limited to a defined set of highly liquid assets, including Russell 1000 stocks, ETFs tracking major indexes, and U.S. Treasuries. Morgan Stanley said last week it had tokenized U.S. stocks and Treasuries through the service.

Tokens issued on Solana "will retain the same investor protections, ownership rights and regulatory safeguards that apply to traditionally held securities," said Brian Steele, president of DTCC Clearing & Securities Services.

Solana has been actively courting traditional finance in recent months, with Solana Foundation head of institutional Nick Ducoff arguing that, "Institutions choose Solana because it already runs real financial activity at scale." He added that institutions are "already issuing, settling and deploying capital" on the network, in a tweet shared by Solana's official account.

Last month, the Solana Foundation unveiled an open standard for institutional settlement developed with input from J.P. Morgan, and the network completed its Alpenglow upgrade, cutting the time it takes for transactions to become final to roughly 150 milliseconds.

Solana is also lining up more venues for tokenized stocks. Trading platform Formation has notified the SEC of plans to trade tokenized U.S. stocks on Solana, starting with Galaxy and Forward Industries.

#5048. How $10,000 in stablecoins would have gained €420 without earning interest

A fixed dollar-token balance would have gained 4.9% in euros from September 1 to November 13 before costs. A stronger euro can reverse that effect.

A dollar stablecoin can keep its peg while the euro spending value of a European saver’s balance moves sharply. At a perfect $1 peg, an unchanged holding would have gained about 4.9% in euros between September 1 and November 13, 2026, using European Central Bank reference rates and excluding costs.

The ECB’s household stablecoin analysis puts that currency exposure in context. Its experimental 2025 survey evidence identifies ownership of dollar tokens among euro area consumers. The subsequent exchange-rate comparison illustrates a separate point: stability against the dollar does not promise stability against the currency used to pay the rent.

The bulletin draws on Consumer Expectations Survey modules from August and November 2025 across the 11 largest euro area countries. In August, 5% of consumers reported stablecoin ownership by themselves or household members, while 13% reported crypto ownership.

Among respondents with crypto holdings, 17% reported USDT, 12% USDC and 10% the euro-denominated EURC. Those percentages measure how common ownership was among crypto-holding respondents. They reveal no token’s share of invested capital. Respondents could select several assets, and the crypto-holder subsample comprised 1,286 people.

The ownership observations date to 2025. The ECB flags small samples, questionnaire sensitivity and possible misreporting. It also says the survey does not directly report how assets were used, so the figures cannot establish payment adoption or tell us what households earned.

The two-date illustration takes September 1 as its chosen baseline. Different holding periods can produce different currency returns. The ECB’s dollar reference-rate history shows $1.1590 per euro on September 1 and $1.1052 on November 13, the latest working-day observation available for this comparison.

With fewer dollars needed to buy one euro, the same dollar balance translated into more euros. For 10,000 unchanged tokens worth exactly $1 each, the illustrative value rose from €8,628 to €9,048, a gain of about €420 before costs. Dividing 1.1590 by 1.1052 and subtracting one gives a 4.9% increase.

That entire illustrated gain comes from currency movement. Token quantity and dollar price are held constant, with no interest earned. Actual households’ returns would depend on their holdings, timing and costs. The ECB also publishes its rates for information and discourages transactional use, so retail conversion quotes can differ from these translation values.

Illustrative unchanged 10,000-token balance at a perfect $1 peg, using September 1 and November 13, 2026 ECB reference rates.

The assumed peg and unchanged token count hold the dollar value at $10,000 on both dates.

The November 13 rate translates the same dollars into about €420 more than the September 1 rate, before costs.

The euro value rises 4.87% in this chosen interval through currency translation alone, before costs.

Hypothetical unchanged balance and exact $1 peg, with no yield, fees, spreads or taxes. ECB rates are informational, not executable quotes. The chosen two-date window is not a household holding period or an estimate of survey respondents’ profits. No APY comparison or forecast.

Euro value = 10,000 / USD per EUR: 10,000/1.1590 = 8,628.127696; 10,000/1.1052 = 9,048.136084. Difference €420.008388; return 1.1590/1.1052-1 = 4.867897%. Values rounded to cents and return to 2 decimals. Bars start at zero on a common 0-10,000 scale within each currency; currency units differ between panels.

Hypothetical unchanged balance and exact $1 peg, with no yield, fees, spreads or taxes. ECB rates are informational, not executable quotes. The chosen two-date window is not a household holding period or an estimate of survey respondents’ profits. No APY comparison or forecast.

More generally, gross euro value equals token quantity multiplied by the token’s dollar price, divided by dollars per euro. Income can change the quantity or value of a position; a depeg changes the dollar price; exchange rates change its euro translation. Conversion costs reduce what is available to spend. A stronger euro can reverse the currency effect even if the dollar peg remains intact.

A separate stablecoin-yield study by DefiLlama Research, published November 12, examined a November 9 snapshot of 98 stablecoin pools with at least $50 million supplied, no token incentives over the preceding 30 days and a recorded 30-day base annual percentage yield (APY).

It reported a median base APY of 4.1%. Forty-eight pools exceeded the study’s 4.2% three-month Treasury benchmark, dated November 5; that selected group’s median was 5.4%.

These are annualized yield measures based on a trailing 30-day window. They cannot be compared as realized returns with the September-to-November currency gain. They do show why a quoted income rate gives only part of the euro holder’s picture. DefiLlama links higher premiums to additional credit, trading, liquidity or underlying-asset risks, alongside the risks of using smart contracts.

Bare token ownership is different again. Circle’s European Economic Area (EEA) USDC white paper says USDC itself generates no interest for holders and gives them no entitlement to reserve income. Earning a DeFi yield requires a separate position with its own terms and risks.

Redemption also needs a currency and an access route. Circle describes USDC as redeemable one-for-one for dollars. Although Circle Mint is institutional, eligible EEA retail holders have a separate route through Circle France under its MiCA redemption policy, subject to identity and transaction checks and an EEA bank account able to receive USD. Third-party bank conversion or incoming-payment fees may apply.

A holder saving for euro expenses therefore carries a currency exposure alongside peg and investment risks. Someone setting aside tokens for a dollar expense or offsetting a dollar liability may have a different net exposure. The relevant question is what the balance will buy in the currency the holder actually needs.

Mason Lynaugh, executive director of Stand With Crypto, joins BMTV to talk through what the midterms mean for Bitcoin and crypto.

Mason Lynaugh, executive director of Stand With Crypto, joins BMTV to talk through what the midterms mean for Bitcoin and crypto. #5046. The 7 Best Head Shavers for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Get the chrome dome of your dreams with these scalp shavers.

AS MEN, THE decision to go bald isn’t always one that’s made for us (thanks, genetics). But how you deal with hair loss is entirely in your hands. Sure, there are some viable hair loss treatments and shampoos for thinning hair that we certainly back. For many men, it's easier to just bite the bullet and shave their hair completely to offset any future thinning woes. If you are one of these men, more power to you! Hell, some men do it even if they’re not experiencing hair loss—and that’s cool, too. Investing in a quality head shaver will double down on the convenience factor of being bald by making the entire process seamless.

When you do choose to shave your head, the tools you use to do it are paramount. That’s where the best head shavers come in. These high-tech gadgets are specifically designed to make shaving your head easier, whether it’s through a multi-head ergonomic design or close-cutting technology (or both).

Far easier than heading to the barbershop every few days, these electric shavers are meant to be used at home. Think of them as an easier, safer, and quicker alternative to carefully taking a razor to your dome. But before investing in a shaver, there are a few key factors to keep in mind to ensure you select the absolute best one for you.

This tiny but powerful shaver is designed to give your scalp the closest shave possible, whether you prefer to do it dry, wet, or with the aid of other products. The five ScalpSafe shaving heads wrap around the curves of your head for a microscopically close shave, and the additional attachments, like a pre-shave exfoliation brush and precision trimmer, are nice bonuses.

Our editors also love that it pairs nicely with our favorite shaving creams and pre-shave oils, in case you want an even deeper cut. Its portable design makes it easy to carry in your luggage, though its travel case is sold separately. Not to mention, the five heads of this shaver definitely give an incredibly close shave—as close as the Remington and the Braun, both of which we found to be top of the heap in our testing process.

We also appreciate the additional attachments that this one comes with, unlike the Remington, particularly the pre-shave exfoliating brush, which not only helps give a closer shave, but also feels pretty damn good on your dome (you’ll want to only use this if you have a tiny bit of stubble though—the bristles aren’t long enough to reach through longer hair).

In theory, the trimmer attachment and the accompanying guards are great if you want to trim your beard (the brand also says you can use it to trim your body and other areas), but we found that the design of the device makes that difficult. Since it’s meant to be held in the palm of your hand, it’s not as easy to use on your face as a more traditional razor design like the Braun or even the Andis. We would probably skip that and relegate this device to only our heads, which, at a comparable price point to other models like the Remington, is OK.

Read More: How to Give Yourself a Buzzcut

If you’re in a rush, this easy-to-use shaver may be your answer. Thanks to the pivoting shaver heads that hug each curve of your head, the brand says that this device can shave your entire head in just two minutes.

After testing the Remington Balder Pro for over a year, we can safely say that it easily gave us a head shave in less than five minutes, which is great for guys who cut their dome weekly. We love the hair capture chamber, which collects hair for easy cleanup, and its non-slip grip gives you extra control when you're mowing through your head.

Keep in mind that this is designed only for head shaving, so if you’re looking for a more multi-purpose solution, you’ll want to go with a more traditional electric shaver like the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus. And since there aren’t any additional attachments like the kind that come with others, like the Freebird, you’re really only going to use this to give your head a smooth, clean shave (which it is frankly very good at doing).

The price is comparable to other head shavers, but we found that the performance outmatches them, so it’s a great investment if you’re a guy who shaves his head often and doesn’t mind having a separate tool just for that task.

If you’re not the smooth-shave type, but still want to give yourself a close buzz without heading to the barber, the Shortcut Pro delivers. With multiple length options via interchangeable combs, this shaver allows you to try different buzz looks on your own.

As the product image suggests, the Shortcut Pro is super compact, which makes it great for tossing in a Dopp kit and taking on trips. The feel of the shaver takes a second to get used to, but once you learn how to wield it, you'll find it does a solid job of staying cut-free while providing a solid shave.

It’s worth repeating that this won’t give you a close, clean shave, but it is handy if you like more of a stubble look. The design isn’t perfect and is less ergonomic than the Remington or one of the similarly designed shavers, but once you get the hang of it, it’s pretty foolproof.

Our one gripe is that because of the curved design, which is nice for hugging the shape of your head, it’s a bit difficult for detailed work around your ears or cleaning up your neck. A more traditional clipper is better for those things, but that’s a small price to pay for the convenience this one offers.

Like Braun’s previous versions, the Series 9 Pro+ has proven to be effective in performance. Not only is it one of our favorite head shavers, but it’s seen as the “Rolls-Royce of shaving instruments” by Faheem Alexander, barber and owner of Faheem's Hands of Precision in Philadelphia.“I highly recommend [it] because of the unparalleled ease and comfort it provides while also ensuring a super close shave,” he says. “The accompanying portable charging case makes this super easy to throw in a bag and get numerous weeks of shaves without plugging it in.”

During our trial run, we found out that the fast-speed device can cut up to 40,000 cuts per minute. Thanks to its waterproof capability, you can use it in the shower for a refreshing shaving experience. We also love that the device comes with a SmartCare center, which maintains the quality for longer use and makes cleaning up a breeze.

While this isn’t technically a head shaver in the way the two Remingtons or Freebird are, we found in our testing that it performs just as well at shaving your head as it does at shaving your face—it is our best electric razor.

What that means to us is that if you’re looking to streamline the number of devices you have in your arsenal, but don’t want to sacrifice power or efficacy, this is an ideal option. It’s expensive—as the Rolls-Royce of shaving instruments is expected to be—but if you’re using it for multiple things like shaving your head and face, that helps justify the cost a bit more.

Ever wonder how your barber gets such a close shave when he’s doing skin fades or cleaning up your neck? Enter this foil shaver, which is hard to beat when it comes to closeness. Not to mention, it’s a go-to for plenty of barbers. Speaking of which, Alexander gives the Andis tool his stamp of approval because it works efficiently for shaving experiences at home and in the barbershop.

It operates well on battery, delivering up to 80 minutes of run time on a single charge—a duration that’s twice as long as others on this list. The price point may be higher than most on this list, but the results make up for the difference.

This is definitely a classic for a reason—it really gets the job done with an incredibly smooth shave. However, it’s aggressive and not the gentlest experience, especially if you’re just beginning with it. Theoretically, you can use this on your face and other areas, too, but we found that the shaving experience is too harsh for us to use anywhere but our head and neck. You’ll also likely want to finish with some sort of lotion or moisturizer to minimize potential irritation.

Manscaped is one of the most consistent brands in men’s grooming, and this head shaver is a perfect example of why. It simply gets the basics right for a more enjoyable, less irritating shave. The grip, which invites palming, is super user-friendly, making moving the blades along your head easy with minimal effort (or risk of dropping it).

The brand’s signature SkinSafe blade guards make cuts and nicks rare, while the magnetic connection makes clean-up and replacements easy. With a 9,500 RPM motor, it shaves smoothly and efficiently. We found it also required minimal passes to get a full shave. Adding to its user-friendliness, the Dome Shaver Pro battery lasts up to 90 minutes and is USB-C chargeable. Plus, it’s waterproof and includes a sturdy hard-shell travel case.

This head shaver from the always reliable Philips Norelco is a great choice if you’re looking for a smooth, comfortable shave without the hassle. Its 360-degree flexing head follows the contours of your scalp, while the 36 self-sharpening ComfortCut blades deliver an even shave without putting unnecessary pressure on your skin.

The ergonomic grip makes it easy to maneuver, while the PowerAdapt Sensor automatically adjusts power to match hair density as you go. With up to 90 minutes of cordless use, water resistance, and a convenient travel case, it’s a reliable option for both everyday grooming and travel.

Most head shavers feature multiple razor heads to help hug the contours of your head so you can easily navigate areas that are hard to see. The multiple razor heads can also help limit cuts, as the design adjusts to curved angles much better than a single, straight razor.

For the quickest, most adaptable (read: lowest maintenance) shaving experience, look for devices with shaving heads in the five-to-seven range, like the Freebird FlexSeries or Remington Balder Pro. That being said, don’t fall into the common trap of thinking that more shaving heads automatically equals a more powerful shave, as the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus is one of the most powerful options on the market and only has four shaving blades.

Most head shavers on this list can be used dry, which means as long as your hair is already short enough (no more than a couple of days of growth), you can shave with no moisture or product. What's also great is that some options are waterproof, making your shaving experience in the shower a total breeze and easy to clean up.

Plus, you can use most wet/dry shavers with shaving products, so if you prefer to begin with a pre-shave oil to protect your scalp and then add a shaving cream or lotion to help with gliding. Follow it up by rinsing the product off your head—just make sure to also clean any leftover product from the razor heads before you put it away. However, there are a couple of options we recommend that do not have this capability, so if you’re a dedicated shower shaver, focus solely on the wet/dry devices.

A good cordless head shaver can last as long as 90 minutes, which means you can go a whole week without charging the battery. They also unlock the ability to shave in the shower or on the road without having to be plugged in. If you're constantly on the move and shave your head regularly, you will find that cordless options offer lots of convenience and save even more time.

Even before joining the bald brotherhood, most of us have all had an electric razor or beard trimmer die out before we've finished the job. Nobody wants to sport a half-trimmed beard or uneven body hair, but the absolute last spot you'll want an uneven shave is on your dome, as it's the hardest to hide.

To avoid walking around with a patchy skull, keep battery life in mind when choosing an electric shaver. Consider how long you typically take to shave your entire head—and how often you tend to charge devices—before finalizing your decision.

The first question to ask is: Does this shaver come with a case included? If yes, then you're going to want to look at what type of case it is. For frequent travelers, a carrying case made to fit neatly in a Dopp kit or luggage should be a priority. However, if you're just looking for something to store it in, you can allow for more size, given that it'll more easily hold every attachment or replacement piece, so there won't be any long search involved when needed.

For the past four years, Men's Health's grooming writers and editors have tested over 15 head shavers to determine the best-performing options for men. We also spoke with the barber and owner of Faheem’s Hands of Precision in Philadelphia, Faheem Alexander, who has put dozens of top-selling head shavers to the test and evaluated their effectiveness, durability, and ease of use.

In addition to all of this expertise and hands-on experience, we researched and dug into the top head shavers on the market to determine which to test. Following that extensive research and testing process, we landed on these seven best head shavers for men.

#5045. Tether wants its gold token to rival ETFs

New institutional trading and borrowing routes put Tether Gold closer to traditional finance, but access and cash-out terms still matter.

Anchorage Digital’s support for Tether Gold gives eligible institutional clients routes to sell or borrow against XAUT as Paolo Ardoino promotes it as a gold-ETF challenger. The competitive test is how readily those routes deliver funds at the size and price a holder needs.

In Tether’s November 12 announcement, its CEO said he believes XAUT is on track to become “the first true competitor to the gold ETF market.” A day earlier, Anchorage announced custody, principal-desk trading and collateral support for the gold-backed token. Like gold-trust shareholders, token holders still depend on counterparties to turn that exposure into funds.

Tether said KPMG U.S. audited issuer TG Commodities S.A. de C.V.’s financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, issuing an unqualified opinion. The announced audit concerns that entity and year, rather than all current Tether reserves or today’s trading and financing terms.

For eligible clients, desk-sale proceeds come from the trading counterparty. Anchorage advertises USD or USDT borrowing against bank-custodied XAUT through arrangements with other clients. Borrowing preserves gold exposure but creates debt; the announcement does not establish bank-funded lending. It also specifies neither a universal sale settlement currency nor a fiat-withdrawal timetable.

Anchorage says it holds XAUT at Anchorage Digital Bank in the US or Anchorage Digital Singapore. The group’s footer names Anchorage Hold LLC as digital-asset trading provider, Anchorage Digital NY LLC for New York agency trading and A1 Ltd. as a principal-trading business. It does not identify one universal trade-contract entity.

Access is institutional, with limited high-net-worth availability and further requirements for certain trading. Custodied tokens lack Anchorage guarantees and FDIC or SIPC protection. Custody therefore provides neither an insured gold deposit nor assured liquidity.

Anchorage’s notice says US persons cannot purchase or redeem XAUT with TG Commodities. The issuer’s terms contain a qualification: US counterparties qualifying as eligible contract participants, a regulatory category, may be accepted at Tether Gold’s sole discretion. Direct purchases and redemptions also require verified issuer-customer status.

Platform eligibility, issuer eligibility and issuer acceptance are separate gates. Neither institutional access at Anchorage nor eligible-contract-participant status alone establishes the issuer’s acceptance. Anchorage’s notice addresses issuer transactions, rather than a blanket ban on permitted secondary trading or custody.

Even an eligible, verified issuer customer does not have an unconditional cash buyback. The terms describe whole-bar redemption for delivery in Switzerland. Instead of taking delivery, a customer can request that Tether Gold attempt a sale to a gold dealer or broker. Only a successful sale produces fiat proceeds, less fees; Tether Gold has no obligation to repurchase the tokens or bullion. That route also needs a buyer.

The iShares Gold Trust product page describes IAU shares trading on NYSE Arca through brokerage accounts. For an ordinary share sale, a market buyer supplies the money through the brokerage transaction. The trust is not paying the retail holder cash for redeeming a share.

Its currently linked prospectus, dated December 22, 2022, reserves creation and redemption of baskets to authorized participants, with gold exchanged for shares. Retail sale access and direct redemption access are different rights in this structure as well.

Borrowing without selling is also available within conventional brokerage arrangements, subject to approval. Fidelity’s margin FAQ lists ETFs held for at least 30 days as eligible collateral, with special security and account requirements, and says checkwriting, bank cards and bill payments can create or increase margin debt. That general policy establishes neither IAU-specific approval nor a particular borrowing limit.

Ardoino’s ETF challenge ultimately turns on usable access: a client who qualifies, a counterparty willing to transact and terms that deliver the funds required. Custody and collateral support create routes. Their availability at the needed size and price is the next test.

#5044. Every Lululemon Shoe Ranked: I Tested Them All, and I Have Thoughts

After putting Lululemon’s full shoe lineup to the test, here’s how each pair ranked.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Lululemon set the bar high for athleisure with its buttery-soft leggings, and continues to deliver on that front. However, since it had always been primarily an athletic wear brand, it wasn’t part of the running shoe or walking shoe conversation. But that changed in 2022 when Lululemon expanded into footwear. Since then, the brand has slowly built a following in that category, too.

I originally tried a pair of Lululemon sneakers a few months ago after reading rave reviews, but quickly stopped wearing them because they felt too snug at my usual size. But I kept seeing positive feedback from other people, making me wonder if I wrote them off too soon. After all, Lululemon is known for careful construction, thoughtful tailoring, and high-quality products.

Like many other shoe brands, each of Lululemon’s sneakers is designed with a specific purpose in mind. The brand’s shoes match Lululemon's overall understated aesthetic. While there are a few bright colors here and there, you also have plenty of neutrals and muted shades to choose from. That alone makes them stand out in a sea of eyeball-searing sneakers.

To see what I was missing beyond looks, I tried each of Lululemon’s athletic shoes—BeyondFeel, Split Shift, Wildfeel, and Chargefeel 3—to see which is the best. And since it’s best to know what you’re getting into before you grab a pair just because it matches your favorite gym outfit, I get into the details about each shoe model below. I was surprised at how wide of a range the brand offers: There’s a Lululemon sneaker for just about anything. Still, one had to come out on top. These are the best Lululemon shoes, ranked, based on months of testing.

The BeyondFeel is the shoe I originally passed on before because it ran snug. So, PSA: Consider sizing up if you prefer a roomy fit or have wide feet. While Lululemon says online that these fit true to size, that wasn't the case for me. Once I went up half a size, I was hooked.

The BeyondFeel is Lululemon's max cushioned shoe, so you can think of it like a Hoka Bondi 9 or On Cloudmonster 3. It's designed for everyday use. Think: running errands, power walking, actual running—it's all comfortable in the BeyondFeel.

I noticed a difference from my daily trainers the second I slipped my feet inside. The best way to describe the feeling is like the first time I put on a pair of Align leggings. I was immediately comfortable, with no chafing, pinching, or any other issues.

This shoe has a nice, roomy toe box, giving your feet plenty of room to swell naturally as you go about your day or rack up the mileage. It also has a stable heel and good grip although, heads up: The shoes may squeak a little when you first wear them inside.

Lululemon designed the BeyondFeel differently for women vs. men, adding an extra 2 millimeters of foam at the forefoot to take some pressure off the knees and hips. I wouldn't wear the BeyondFeel for long runs, though—it doesn't have much energy return, which is that slight bouncy feeling you may get in a shoe. But I was happy to log a few miles in them here and there, along with wearing them for weight training and just running errands. Their stylish look and comfortable feel make them a good choice for nearly everyone.

The Split Shift is Lululemon's neutral everyday running shoe, which is another way of saying it's a good shoe for most runners. The first thing you'll notice is how lightweight the shoe is. At 7.8 ounces, it's not the lightest shoe ever made, but it definitely won't feel like your feet are dragging you down when you're logging higher mileage. This sneaker has an equally breezy upper, giving it an overall airy feel.

I really appreciate the springiness of these shoes. It's not so much that it feels like you're running on mini trampolines, but there's a good energy return here to help propel you forward with each step. That's definitely a noticeable change from the BeyondFeel, which has pretty much no energy return by comparison. There's a gusseted tongue that gently hugs your ankle, along with some extra padding around the ankle that prevents rubbing. The outsole doesn't feel as grippy as the BeyondFeel, but it's a good choice for everyday road running.

My only complaint with the Split Shift is that the toe box runs a little narrow. I'm used to running in shoes with a wide toe box, and the Split Shift's smaller width across the toes means they probably won't be my go-to for everyday miles. Like the BeyondFeel, I'd suggest going up a half size if you like a roomy toe box or have wide feet.

Lululemon's Chargefeel 3 looks different from the brand's other shoes out of the box. It has an hourglass shape, with a narrow middle, more room at the toes, and an exaggerated base at the heel for stability. That shape is intentional, since this shoe is made for cross-training, hybrid, and HIIT workouts. The Chargefeel 3 is on the lighter end of weight for a gym shoe at 8 ounces, and it feels light on your feet. Still, it has everything you want in a shoe you'll be doing cross-training in, like a locked-in feeling in the heel, snug laces, and ability to handle lateral movements.

The grip on this shoe is impressive. I was able to stop cleanly while doing direction-changing indoor sprints at the gym, with no squeaking. The shoe also features a ShiftFoam midsole for a little energy return. Its not nearly as bouncy as the Split Shift, though—but you don't want that in a shoe you'll be doing hybrid workouts in anyway.

The Chargefeel 3 has a 6mm heel-to-toe drop, which may be high for those looking for a neutral strength training shoe, so it might not be ideal for lifting. It’s laser-cut mesh helps tamp down on foot sweat, along with Nulu fabric heel lining to mimic the feel of your favorite leggings.

And if you're looking for a running shoe, scroll up. This is really a gym shoe that you can do a little running in in a pinch—not something you want to do any significant mileage in. And while the Chargefeel 3 made me feel locked-in and secure during gym workouts, it's not so comfortable that I'd wear this shoe outside of exercise. If you're looking for a dedicated hybrid shoe, though, it's worth a look.

Some athletic shoe brands will slap deep lugs on a sneaker and call it a trail shoe without addressing other needs. But it's clear that Lululemon's Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

There's a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you're going down. Like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. That wasn't a huge deal on shorter runs, but it started to annoy me on longer runs. Like many others on this list, I'd consider going up a half size.

My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that's pretty common in a trail shoe. (It got better with time and more wear.) It's also worth noting that the Wildfeel isn't the most breathable shoe you'll find, and my socks were a little sweatier than usual because of it. None of these are dealbreakers. But it also meant the Wildfeel was my least favorite shoe in Lululemon's lineup.

To choose the best Lululemon shoes, I put each through regular testing over several months. I used each shoe on a near-daily basis for weeks, making sure to test it for the way it was designed. So, I wore the Wildfeel on trails and the Split Shift on daily training runs. During each testing session, I took notes on the shoe's fit, traction, stability, and overall comfort. From there, I ranked each shoe based on its testing results, along with how well it matched up to their intended use.

The best Lululemon shoe for running depends on the type of running you plan to do. If you’re in search of a neutral everyday trainer, the Split Shift is a good choice. It’s lightweight and slightly bouncy, giving you plenty of support and cushioning over daily miles. The BeyondFeel is another solid option. It’s highly cushioned for maximum comfort, making it a better choice for shorter runs.

The best Lululemon shoe for HIIT workouts is the Chargefeel 3. This sneaker has a unique hourglass shape to create a locked-in feel you’ll appreciate during HIIT workouts, along with a wide base for stability. The shoe’s grip is impressive, allowing you to stop quickly and change directions during indoor workouts.

Lululemon used to offer the Strongfeel shoe for strength training, but it’s been discontinued. Now, the Chargefeel 3 is the best option for many strength training workouts due to its wide base and stable platform. But as noted above, the shoe has a higher heel-to-toe drop of 6mm, so it’s not ideal for moves like deadlifts. So if lifting is your priority, you might want to consider a more neutral shoe for optimal biomechanics.

Lululemon often says online that its shoes fit true to size, but that wasn't my experience. I don't have wide feet, but I do appreciate a roomy toe box to accommodate the natural foot swelling that happens on workouts and runs. Most Lululemon shoes tend to run narrow across the toe box. If you have wide feet or just prefer more room to spread your toes, consider going up a size.

#5043. Robinhood’s Crypto Trading Volume Falls 48% in October as Event Contracts More Than Double

Crypto trading on Robinhood fell by almost half from a year ago in October, the company said Thursday, as customers traded $17 billion of digital assets while their bets on event contracts more than doubled.

The $17 billion figure was down 21% from September and 48% from October 2025, when crypto notional volume reached $32.5 billion. It covers both the flagship Robinhood app and Bitstamp, the crypto exchange the company bought in 2025.

Volume in the Robinhood app fell to $6.8 billion, down 24% from September and 51% from a year earlier. Bitstamp handled $10.2 billion, down 18% month over month and 45% year over year.

Average daily crypto volume across both platforms came to $548 million, compared with $713 million in September and about $1.05 billion a year ago. Daily average crypto trades slipped to about 700,000 from 900,000 in September and 1.1 million in October 2025.

The contrast with Robinhood’s prediction markets business is stark. Customers traded 5.9 billion event contracts in October, up 5% from September and 136% from the 2.5 billion traded a year earlier. Average daily volume reached 190 million contracts.

Robinhood counts crypto and prediction markets on the same 31-day calendar, since both trade every day, so the comparison is apples to apples. Event contracts let users bet on outcomes such as elections, sports and economic data, and October’s tally covered the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

That growth has drawn scrutiny in Washington. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee in January, plans to crack down on prediction markets and election betting platforms.

The rest of Robinhood’s brokerage held up better than crypto. Equity notional volume rose 2% from a year earlier to $325 billion, and options contracts traded climbed 8% to 289 million. Margin balances reached $22.9 billion, up 39% year over year.

Funded customers rose by about 130,000 in the month to 28.9 million, and net deposits came to $15.1 billion. Total platform assets slipped 3% from September to $383 billion but were up 12% from a year earlier.

Robinhood did not say why crypto activity fell. The release, like all of the company’s monthly updates, is unaudited and preliminary.

The slump in Robinhood’s crypto numbers lines up with a broader retreat by retail traders. Bitcoin ended September near $83,500 and has slid since, falling below $70,000 early Friday for the first time since August as a hot inflation report raised bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Institutional demand has cooled alongside it. U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds posted a sixth straight day of net outflows on Thursday, and BlackRock’s IBIT, the largest of them, bled about $2 billion over nine sessions through Wednesday. Spot bitcoin ETFs have now erased their net inflows for 2026.

Crypto trading generates transaction revenue for Robinhood, so lower volume generally means fewer fees, even when assets on the platform keep growing. The company reports full fourth-quarter results early next year, and October’s figures are the first look at how the quarter started.

The company has kept expanding its crypto footprint anyway. In October, Robinhood won a license in Dubai to offer bitcoin and stock trading in the Middle East starting in 2027.

Robinhood also said cash and deposit balances fell 20% in October to $16.4 billion, mostly because customers were net buyers, and that the decline has largely reversed in early November. November’s operating data will show whether this month’s selloff below $70,000 brought crypto traders back or pushed more of them toward event contracts.

#5042. SoFi Brings Its Bank-Issued Stablecoin to Polygon’s Payments Stack

SoFi Brings Its Bank-Issued Stablecoin to Polygon’s Payments Stack

SoFi is widening the reach of its digital dollar, bringing SoFiUSD, the first stablecoin issued by a U.S. national bank, onto Polygon’s payments infrastructure as banks and fintechs push stablecoins deeper into everyday money movement.

Polygon Labs said Thursday that SoFiUSD is now live on Polygon Open Money Stack, a payments layer that bundles fiat on- and off-ramps, embedded wallets and cross-chain settlement into a single integration.

The move adds Polygon alongside Ethereum and Solana, the networks SoFiUSD already runs on, and lets SoFi’s more than 17 million members buy, sell, hold, and convert the token on Polygon directly in the SoFi app, without opening a separate crypto wallet or manually bridging assets between chains.

“SoFi is well positioned to bring stablecoins into mainstream finance because it combines the regulatory foundation of a national bank with the reach of a major consumer and enterprise technology platform,” said Marc Boiron, CEO of Polygon Labs.

The expansion lands as stablecoins move beyond crypto trading into the plumbing used to settle card payments, pay businesses, and send money across borders.

On Polygon Open Money Stack, SoFiUSD joins USDC, USDT and PayPal’s PYUSD, and can connect to the wallets, banking rails, and local currencies businesses need for payouts, settlement and cross-border transfers, opening up uses well beyond consumer trading.

The token is redeemable one-to-one for U.S. dollars and issued by SoFi Bank, which is regulated by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

SoFi launched SoFiUSD late last year across Ethereum and Solana as the first stablecoin from a U.S. national bank, and it already settles the company’s entire card program over Mastercard’s network. The firm has been building out a broader digital-money suite, recently launching SoFi Earn, a tokenized deposit that pays 4.40% yield and converts one-to-one into SoFiUSD.

For Polygon, the addition deepens a payments business that has become one of the network’s calling cards.

Polygon recently extended Open Money Stack to Solana, and the chain has processed more than $3 trillion in lifetime stablecoin transfer volume, according to the company. Visa and Mastercard support stablecoin settlement on Polygon, while Stripe uses it to route USDC payments for merchants in more than 150 countries.

SoFiUSD is a payment stablecoin, not a bank deposit, and is not FDIC- or SIPC-insured, bank-guaranteed or legal tender.

Part of the reason I wore this for my 10K race was simply that it looks better on me than just about every other workout tank I own. I think that’s mostly thanks to the compression of the garment, which gives it a smoothing effect and helps make me look snatched.

It has a low scoop neck cut with a racerback silhouette. The longline fit hits a bit lower on your torso than a regular bra would, giving it the look of a cropped tank with the fit of a supportive bra. I love that I can throw this on without worrying about an extra layer and feel a little more covered up than when I head to the gym in a regular sports bra. That said, sometimes I wish it were a bit longer, but most of my workout bottoms are high-waisted, so it ends up feeling long enough.
