#4951. The 6 Best On Shoes for Walking of 2026, Tested By Fitness Editors and Podiatrists

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a Women’s Health style writer, I regularly test the latest releases from all the major sneaker brands. On kicks are some of my favorites, and our editors and A-list celebs love ‘em too (including Zendaya). The Swiss brand has seen impressive growth over the past year, becoming a major competitor among sneaker giants like Nike and Adidas. On’s signature CloudTec cushioning not only makes you feel like you’re “walking on clouds,” but it’s also right on trend and a major style statement for wellness girlies.

We've named these kicks some of the best running shoes for plantar fasciitis, but after vigorous testing, we absolutely love On shoes for walking, too. Podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM, says he walks around the city daily in his On sneakers because they make him feel supported and comfortable and accommodate his Dr. Scholl's insoles. "Thanks to the thicker sole and rounded heel, they provide that perfect mix of function, stability, and cushion without sacrificing any category," he says.

On has a large roster of comfortable sneakers, so it can be tricky to know where to start to find the perfect pair. That's why we tapped Schaeffer, podiatrist Daniel Geller, DPM, and Women's Health fitness editors to give us the lowdown on what to look for when shopping for the best On Cloud shoes for walking: in this case, weight, cushion, stability, and heel-to-toe drop.

Keep reading to see our favorites, and be sure to check out our 4-Week Walking Plan for the perfect workout to break in your new kicks.

After testing several pairs of On shoes, the Cloudrunner 3—a cushier, more supportive upgrade from the Cloudrunner 2—takes the top spot for a few key reasons. Executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos has tested more than a dozen On shoes and says the Cloudrunner 3 has become a go-to in her sneaker collection lately. That’s because the shoe has a relatively lightweight feel with tons of stability.

That balance comes from the sole, which is made with On’s Helion Superfoam. This material, made from thermoplastic polyurethane, blends firm and flexible foam components to create a lightweight, responsive, and well-cushioned feel. The mix of stiffer and softer sections absorbs impact from every step and actually helps propel you forward. The Cloudrunner 3 is actually a touch heavier than its predecessor (by only 0.7 ounces), but we chalk it up to the upgraded plush heel collar and wider base that offer a bit more comfort and stability. I’ve noticed this shoe is super durable, holding up to months of wear and tear on city sidewalks. During my walks in this shoe, I appreciate that I don’t feel overly bouncy, but the cushioning is still noticeable and light enough to help me feel grounded.“At nine months pregnant, I need to prioritize stability and comfort over everything else in a sneaker right now, and the On Cloudrunner 3s delivered for me,” Andriakos says. “It feels firm and supportive (and not overly cushioned), which has noticeably reduced my pelvic and low back pain when I’m on my feet all day and walking a lot.” She’s also been wearing it for hybrid strength-and-cardio workouts, and while it’s not a super-flat traditional lifting shoe, the fairly neutral sole and structured shape and feel make it surprisingly versatile. “Plus, the toe box is on the wider side and roomy enough for my swollen feet, so my toes can actually breathe,” Andriakos adds.

After about four months of testing an alarming amount of shoes, the On Cloudtilt Remix is my everyday go-to. That’s because this sneaker takes everything we love about the original Cloudtilt and gives it a fashion-forward upgrade with a techy upper designed with “X-ray layers,” or semi-transparent mesh overlays that look super sleek.

This shoe is basically built for walking, too, thanks to the CloudTec Phase midsole, a walking-focused cushioning system designed so each “cloud” compresses in sequence, delivering a smooth, plush ride. The result is an exceptionally smooth heel-to-toe transition that feels natural and effortless during long days on your feet. It also has a moderate 7 mm heel-to-toe drop, meaning it distributes weight evenly throughout the lower body and helps keep the foot in a neutral walking position, making it a pretty universal pick.

Underfoot, the cushioning lands squarely in the Goldilocks zone. The Helion superfoam provides plenty of impact absorption, but the ride never feels overly soft or marshmallow-like. Instead, it delivers a lightly responsive, cushioned feel that keeps your feet comfortable during long walks, travel days, and hours of sightseeing without sacrificing ground feel or stability. Lightweight, stylish, and genuinely built for all-day movement, the Cloudtilt Remix is the On sneaker I reach for when I want my shoes to work as hard as the rest of my outfit. The sleek, streamlined look is super easy to style with everything from tennis skirts to joggers to track pants. If you ask me, it’s kinda the perfect shoe that combines everything on this list into one sleek kick.

My one note is that I worry about the layered mesh upper being difficult to clean if the shoe gets too dirty. Luckily, I’ve managed to keep it pretty clean, but I avoid wearing this shoe in wet weather or otherwise messy conditions.

Hate tying your shoes? The Cloudnova Form 2 might be your new favorite—thanks to its easy slip-on, slip-off design, which Andriakos swears by. That said, it still has laces if you want to tighten things up for a more secure fit. This is my everyday shoe when I’m heading out the door to run errands or pop out for a walk but don’t feel like wearing anything bulky or something that needs a full lace adjustment (just lazy girl things!). It looks super cute with sweatpants and leggings, and a boxy t-shirt on top.

Comfort-wise, the Cloudnova Form is a win right out of the box. During my testing, I found that there was no break-in period needed (big ups). The moderately-cushioned sole is super balanced, which makes it ideal for long walks and power strolls, and Andriakos especially likes that it doesn’t have the super-prominent “bubble” look that many On shoes are known for. Instead, it has a lower-cut silhouette that feels a bit more grounded and less bouncy.

Another plus: The Form 2 is made with a breathable mesh upper and a soft microfiber tongue, so your feet stay cool and comfortable even on warm or extra-active days. On the downside, it runs small, so it’s a good idea to size it up by half. Also worth noting: it has a high heel-to-toe drop (14 mm), which can put extra stress on the knees and hips. If you deal with pain in those areas, you might want to skip this one.

On only offers wide sizing for certain models, but this shoe has a spacious toe box for a roomy fit. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi has bunions and never experiences pain when wearing it. “Most sneakers that don’t come in wide sizing tend to irritate and rub against my bunions, which makes them throb, but not the Cloudmonster,” she says. “The toe box is surprisingly a perfect fit and lets me walk around for hours pain-free.”

This new version of the shoe delivers a cradling sensation while the foam slightly compresses to conform to your feet. The sensation is pillow-like under the foot while also offering a stable feel. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton notes that it's her all-time fave On walking shoe for its high-stack cushion, meaning it has a very thick foam between your foot and the ground. The 3 gets back to the Cloudmonster’s roots and becomes a good running shoe for intermediate to advanced runners again. That’s thanks to a speedboard that promotes a forward rolling motion, along with the aforementioned maxed cushioning. This has added only a little weight from the last model (6.6 ounces to 8.5), so you don’t have to worry about this shoe holding you back during long walks or runs.

"Whenever I want to feel super comfortable in my shoes but don't want that tight, locked-in feeling like I do when I'm running, the Cloudmonster is my go-to," Appleton says. She wore the shoe while moving into her fourth-floor Brooklyn walk-up, and notes it kept her feet comfortable all day. And while it’s great for getting your steps in, this shoe has that chunky look that’s super on trend right now. I love pairing it with tailored pants and a boxy t-shirt on top for that upgraded activewear vibe.

The heel-to-toe drop is also on the smaller side at six millimeters, which Accardi says distributes impact evenly on the knees, hips, and ankles. “As someone with knee issues, taking the load off my knees is essential, especially post-run,” she says. If you’re a heel striker and don’t struggle with pain in these areas, the Cloudrunner 2 could be a better fit.

If your workouts don’t fit neatly into one category, the On Cloud X 4 is the sneaker you’ll want on standby. Designed specifically for mixed training, it’s comfortable, responsive, and stable, making it equally suited for walking, HIIT training, and gym sessions. Unlike some of On’s chunkier models, the Cloud X 4 has a slightly lower-profile silhouette that looks and feels sleeker on foot, pairing easily with everyday outfits and activewear.

The shoe features On’s signature CloudTec cushioning, which delivers a comfortable, impact-absorbing ride without feeling overly squishy. Andriakos, who logs a high daily step count, says it’s become one of her favorite shoes for long walks because the cushioning feels nice and plush while maintaining a grounded feel. “The mesh upper is super breathable, so my feet don’t feel overheated and sweaty after long walks, and small design details (like the cool X lace pattern from above!) make it feel really polished,” she says.

The supportive lacing system creates a secure, locked-in feel that feels stable during lateral movements and dynamic workouts. “I’ve worn it to HIIT classes, and it feels super supportive, though I’d still opt for a flatter, more structured shoe for traditional lifting,” Andriakos says. The mesh upper is a nice touch, too, keeping things super breathable so your feet don’t get overheated or sweaty on long walks.

The On Cloud 6 Coast is a refreshed take on the brand’s classic On Cloud—but this ultra-lightweight version takes it even further. It keeps all the upgrades of the latest model, including the original slip-on, no-lace design and On’s signature CloudTec cushioning system. The big win here? It weighs in at just 6.5 ounces. That means your ultra-cushioned shoe is now perfect for traveling, long days on your feet, or hot, humid commutes. It’s built with an updated mesh that’s super breathable and ventilated—you can even wear this shoe barefoot!It also features a wider opening for a more inclusive, easy-on fit. I really appreciated this feature as a wide-footed girly. It also has a moderate heel-to-toe drop of 8 mm, making it a great universal walking shoe. Bottom line: this shoe is made to handle just about anything, which makes it a must-have in your rotation.

This shoe has a medium cushion level for that sweet spot that’s comfortable and light on your feet without being overly plush. The CloudTec midsole does a great job absorbing impact, making it a solid choice for everything from sightseeing and airport sprints to casual daily walks. The lightweight build almost disappears on your foot, which is exactly what you want when you’re packing light or spending hours exploring.

The tradeoff for all that packability and featherlight comfort is support. The flexible upper and minimalist construction can feel a bit flimsy compared to more structured walking shoes, especially if you need extra arch support or stability.

On sneakers are extremely comfortable, but Schaeffer says that's because most of its shoes have a bit of weight to them. If a shoe is too lightweight (under four ounces), it sacrifices function and stability, he says. But, don't get it twisted—these don't feel like bricks on your feet either. Most On shoes are between four and 10 ounces, which means they're the perfect medium weight that doesn’t slack on support.

A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer says to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

Support and stability are the number one qualities you should look for in a walking shoe, says Geller. He notes that when arches are supported, you create an "excellent" platform to launch from, meaning the feet are in the ideal position for takeoff and landing. This can help avoid foot injuries down the line.

Geller also says that many good walking shoes, including motion control shoes, will have medial posting—a firm wedge in the arch that holds up the heel—and firm cushioning for more support. "Firmer cushioning will resist the inward roll of the foot [overpronation], controlling the knees and hips better," he says.

If stability is a priority for you, also consider shoes with a broader sole to minimize excess movement. The increased material along the sides and front of your foot creates a wider platform, which is naturally resistant to feet rolling or wobbling, says Geller. In other words, it's a great feature for walkers who overpronate.

"Whenever you’re looking for a good walking shoe, you want to find a great mix of comfort and stability," says Schaeffer. You want a shoe that’s comfortable on your feet, but the level of cushioning will vary depending on your specific foot needs.

Wearing running shoes for walking isn’t inherently bad, but it’s not always the best idea either. Shoes designed specifically for running tend to have significantly more cushioning to absorb the higher impact that comes with each stride. “This isn't necessary for walking and reduces your feel of the ground, which is problematic for those with any balance issues or previous falls," Milica McDowell, a doctor of physical therapy, previously told Women’s Health.

Running shoes often have a very tight fit for higher performance, a narrow toe box, or are highly supported in the arch, which are features a lifestyle walker does not need, says McDowell. That’s why, in most cases, walkers are recommended to opt for a shoe designed specifically for walking (or one labeled for walking and running).

To curate a list of the best On walking shoes, I tested On kicks for two years, alongside fitness contributor Talene Appleton, NASM-CPT, fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi, NASM-CPT, style contributor Lily Wohlner, and executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos.

We wore them during long and short walks for at least several hours at a time. We evaluated each shoe based on:

We found that the new and older winners all provide top-notch comfort, cushioning, support, and stability through all our long walks.

#4949. Traders claim $6 million profit by spotting BitGo’s public pull request and frontrunning memecoin listing

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

A pseudonymous trader claims to have anticipated a memecoin's Robinhood listing, which sent its price soaring, by tracking code changes in BitGo's public repository and Wintermute smart contracts.

A pseudonymous trader said their group profited more than $6 million by buying two Robinhood Chain memecoins ahead of their Robinhood listings after spotting a public BitGo code change and analyzing Wintermute's onchain activity.

The trader, who posts on X as @3i, described their "edge" in an article published on Saturday that has drawn more than 300,000 views. The Block confirmed several of the public records the trader cites and found wallet activity that matches parts of the timeline, though could not verify the profit figures.

Robinhood launched Robinhood Chain, a Layer 2 network built on Arbitrum's tech stack, on July 1. BitGo announced wallet and custody support for the network the same day, while Robinhood has named algorithmic trading firm Wintermute as one of its largest crypto market makers in an SEC filing.

According to 3i, the pair began tracking Wintermute's wallets on Robinhood Chain and BitGo's activity on GitHub after it noticed that Wintermute had been moving tokens to Robinhood about an hour before earlier memecoin listings were announced.

Indeed, a BitGo developer had opened a pull request, or a proposed code change, in the company's public BitGoJS repository on July 27. Included in the code: "Add hoodeth:cashcat (Cash Cat) token to hoodethTokens.ts on the Robinhood Chain." The change was merged the next day.

While Cash Cat was launched on July 1, Robinhood didn't list the token until Aug. 6, ten days after the July 27 pull request was made.

BitGo released a new version of its code on July 29, which included the Cash Cat code change alongside a separate change that added support for 99 Robinhood Chain stock tokens. "The implications of this were huge, as it confirmed my hunch that Robinhood was the one behind this request," 3i wrote. "Why else would cashcat be in there next to their native stock tokens?"

Though 3i said the pair had been buying up the memecoin in the days after the pull request, eventually accumulating 1.5% of the token's overall supply, they had been waiting for a stronger signal to buy even more: Wintermute whitelisting the token, or transferring the token to Robinhood.

The trader claims that on Aug. 3 at 1:48 p.m. ET, their monitoring bot caught Wintermute approving the trading pool. "That was the alert we’d been waiting for," 3i wrote. "The desk had selected a venue to trade the exact coin we were holding."

The pair began buying slowly to avoid drawing attention to their wallets, 3i wrote. But about half an hour later, at 2:19 p.m. ET, a wallet the pair suspected belonged to a Robinhood insider placed an $11,000 limit order for the memecoin. Knowing that other traders were watching the same wallet, the pair abandoned the slow approach and bought more than $1 million worth of Cash Cat at once, bringing their holdings to around 4% of the token's supply, according to 3i.

Per onchain data reviewed by The Block, a wallet made its first Cash Cat purchase at 1:54 p.m. ET on Aug. 3, six minutes after the Wintermute alert 3i describes. After three small buys, the wallet bought about 12 million tokens in two swaps at 2:20 p.m. ET, one minute after the suspected insider's order, before moving the tokens to other wallets. In total, it picked up about 15 million tokens, or 1.5% of the supply.

Onchain analytics firm Bubblemaps flagged the wallet the next morning, noting that it had spent $1.1 million on the memecoin as part of $2.7 million in purchases by a cluster of fresh wallets. While 3i's article claims ownership of the wallets in question, The Block could not independently confirm who controls them.

The Block also identified a Wintermute-labeled contract on Robinhood Chain that keeps a public list of tokens it is approved to trade, which may be one of the three contracts 3i describes that carry that list. However, Cash Cat was not added to that list until around 6:31 a.m. ET on Aug. 5, nearly two days after the signal 3i claims to have caught, but still about 27 hours ahead of Robinhood's listing announcement.

Robinhood announced that Cash Cat was available to trade at 9:31 a.m. ET on Aug. 6, three days after the pair's largest purchase. 3i wrote that while they napped through the token's initial price spike following the listing, the pair still made more than $4 million between them by selling into the frenzy.

3i also claims the pair managed to get ahead of Robinhood employees who were themselves trading the listing. Another pseudonymous trader, clickless, published a separate account on the day of the listing describing a wallet they believed belonged to an insider, which placed a Cash Cat limit order before the announcement and ultimately lost money.

3i said the pair later repeated the trade with PONS, the token of a memecoin launchpad on Robinhood Chain. The trader said they began buying on Aug. 28 and that they and "friends" made $2 million, though the article does not explain how they identified the token.

What looked like a Sept. 2 listing of PONS, however, appeared to have been "some kind of honeypot for Robinhood to catch the insiders," 3i wrote. The trader added that most of the advantage described in the article has since faded.

On Sept. 15, the Department of Justice charged two former Robinhood engineers with commodities fraud and wire fraud for allegedly trading perpetual futures on Hyperliquid ahead of Robinhood listing announcements. Robinhood said at the time that it had investigated the matter and reported it to law enforcement.

The Block has reached out to Robinhood, Wintermute, BitGo and @3i for comment.

#4947. Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Wants to Freeze AI Data Center Boom as Congress Pushes to Expand It

Republican Senator Josh Hawley wants Congress to hit the brakes on new data centers, just as lawmakers are moving forward with legislation intended to make building the infrastructure behind America's AI boom easier.

The Missouri senator called for a nationwide moratorium Wednesday, listing it among five priorities for Senate Republicans during the six weeks before Democrats take control of the chamber.

“Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks?” Hawley wrote on X. His answer included a moratorium on data centers, alongside defunding Planned Parenthood, suspending the gas tax and other Republican priorities.

A spokesperson told Politico that Hawley wants a federal pause until Congress passes a “bill of rights giving taxpayers guarantees of no rate increases.” Hawley has not presented detailed legislation specifying which projects would stop or how long the freeze would last.

Data centers are the warehouses packed with powerful computers that train and operate services such as ChatGPT. Building more AI systems means installing more servers, which requires additional electricity, cooling equipment and often upgrades to local power grids.

Senate Republicans trying to figure out what to do in the next 6 weeks? Here you go:DEFUND Planned ParenthoodMORATORIUM on data centersSUSPEND the gas tax FUND rural hospitals SAVE AMERICA ACT

— Josh Hawley (@HawleyMO) November 11, 2026

The scale helps explain the concern. U.S. data centers consumed an estimated 183 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, according to figures cited by Pew, and that could climb to 426 by 2030. In other words, their annual electricity demand could more than double in six years.

On Monday, the Senate voted 73-25 to advance debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a proposal backed by lawmakers from both parties and President Donald Trump's administration.

The bill would speed federal reviews for energy projects and transmission lines, helping bring new power supplies online. It would also require data center operators to pay the additional grid costs their projects create, rather than shifting those expenses onto ordinary electricity customers.

In practical terms, Congress is considering how to keep construction moving without making households subsidize it. Hawley is asking lawmakers to stop new construction until consumer protections are in place.

His position is not entirely new. In February, Hawley introduced the GRID Act with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, seeking to make new data centers obtain electricity from their own sources rather than relying on existing grid supplies.

He now joins independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in publicly supporting a national pause. Their moratorium proposal goes further, calling for rules addressing AI's effects on workers and public safety as well as the environment.

The politics have shifted quickly. In the November 3 elections, voters backed restrictions on data center development across the country, including local bans and measures requiring public approval before construction.

A Pew Research Center analysis published Wednesday found 60% of Americans uncomfortable with a new data center in their area, including 54% of Republicans and 68% of Democrats. Another survey found 58% disliked political leaders who support building data centers near them.

Opponents worry about rising bills, water consumption and noise. Cities have already imposed restrictions, while OpenAI recently promised to cover electricity and grid costs at future campuses it owns and operates.

Industry supporters see a bigger economic risk. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned last month that a construction moratorium could trigger a recession because so much investment now depends on AI infrastructure.

A federal construction freeze could delay the additional computing capacity that AI companies expect to bring online, along with the power infrastructure built to support it. Existing data centers would not necessarily shut down, but the scope of Hawley's proposed moratorium remains undefined.

Hawley's call does not freeze a single project, and he has not said whether he would support the Sanders bill. For now, the Senate is debating legislation to speed infrastructure approvals, not legislation to ban new data centers.

Crypto liquidations totaled $2.02 billion from 8 a.m. ET Saturday to 8 a.m. ET Sunday, according to CoinGlass's hourly data. Longs accounted for $1.68 billion and shorts for $342.4 million. Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao denied rumors that the world's largest exchange was selling crypto following its recent record-breaking hack on Oct. 29.

"No, Binance did not sell crypto," Zhao wrote in a post on X. He said he had used stablecoins he recently received to buy crypto over the past few days.

Zhao cited withdrawals from U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike as possible reasons for the slide. He also suggested investors could be freeing up cash for Anthropic's planned IPO and pointed to security concerns following the October Binance hack.

U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs saw $1.91 billion in net outflows over seven straight trading days through Friday, as The Block previously reported. Spot ether ETFs shed $398.9 million last week, their seventh consecutive week of withdrawals, approaching their record of eight.

#4942. Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Congress Summons Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Lutnick Over Chip Exports to China

Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC), chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, has asked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, widening a congressional inquiry that has moved from Huang's private life to U.S. controls on chip exports to China. "The American people deserve answers," Scott wrote in a tweet announcing the requests on Thursday evening.

In a letter dated November 12, Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily at a public hearing on December 3 over public reports that "raise significant national security concerns." The committee has jurisdiction over export controls, "including their application to NVIDIA's exports of advanced semiconductors," he wrote. If Huang does not appear, the committee "is prepared to use all tools at our disposal, including subpoenas."

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology.

I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

The American people deserve… pic.twitter.com/Xu1kiNzkhW

— Senator Tim Scott (@SenatorTimScott) November 13, 2026

Scott asked Lutnick to testify on December 10, noting Commerce's "central role in issuing and enforcing export control regulations." A Lutnick spokesperson told NBC News that he had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily," while the White House said President Donald Trump "maintains complete confidence" in Lutnick.

Separately on Thursday, the Republican chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, China and Intelligence committees, Reps. Brian Mast (R-FL), John Moolenaar (R-MI) and Rick Crawford (R-AR), wrote to Huang, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department's under secretary for industry and security.

Huang was asked to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1 and Teter on December 2, with each given until 8 p.m. on Friday to agree or face a subpoena. Kessler, whose bureau administers export controls, was invited to a hearing on December 3.

"As reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and MegaSpeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three chairs said in a statement. They called on Congress to add four chip security bills to the annual defense authorization bill.

It is their second request. A letter dated November 4 had asked Huang to brief the committees on November 18. Mast told reporters on Thursday that Huang had agreed to brief lawmakers, NBC News reported.

At the center of the inquiries is Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. U.S. officials suspected the company of helping Chinese firms get around restrictions on advanced AI chips, The New York Times reported in October. Its sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the Times.

Megaspeed told the Times it had hired outside counsel to conduct an internal investigation. Nvidia has said it complies with U.S. export laws, according to NBC News.

The Times reported that U.S. officials had concluded that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, was a Chinese intelligence asset. China has rejected that as a smear, and Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion on whether she was a spy, according to BBC News.

Jensen Huang admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife and resigned on Thursday. Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

Moolenaar told reporters that Huang had "been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls," Roll Call reported. On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), the Banking Committee's ranking member, and Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) asked Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to preserve records on Nvidia chip exports to China.

China's foreign ministry warned on Friday that tighter U.S. export controls on semiconductors would threaten the stability of global supply chains, Al Jazeera reported.

Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% at $166.19 on Thursday and were up 2.7% at $170.63 in premarket trading early on Friday, according to Yahoo! Finance. The company has lost almost $500 billion in market value since the close on Friday, November 6. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first under interim CEO Colette Kress.

#4937. Bitcoin Drops to $69K On 'Concentrated Liquidation' and 'Weakening' Demand

Bitcoin Drops to $69K On 'Concentrated Liquidation' and 'Weakening' Demand

Leading cryptocurrency Bitcoin has dropped 5.6% on the day, and is currently trading at just over $69,300, per Decrypt data. It comes after the latest consumer price index, or CPI, results came in "hotter than expected," experts said, with the drop was triggered by a "concentrated liquidation."

Bitcoin's plunge took it to a 24-hour low of $67,922, its lowest level since mid-August, when it boosted from $63,000.

"Bitcoin’s drop below $69,000 was directly triggered by a concentrated liquidation of leveraged long positions," Tim Sun, senior analyst at Hashkey, told Decrypt. "Though the deeper issue lies in steadily weakening market demand."

Sun highlighted U.S. Bitcoin spot ETFs recording six consecutive days of net outflows, according to CoinGlass. He also pointed to stablecoin supply shrinking and MSCI removing digital asset treasury firm Strategy from its funds.

"ETFs, stablecoin liquidity, and corporate treasuries have served as the primary capital pillars supporting this Bitcoin rally," Sun said. "With all three coming under simultaneous pressure, the market is losing the marginal buying power that previously propelled prices higher."

Meanwhile, other major cryptocurrencies have also taken a hit. Ethereum has dropped 4.6% on the day to $1,953, BNB has slipped 4.7% to $639.46, and Solana is down 3.1% to $80.47, according to Decrypt data. The global crypto market cap has dropped 4.6% over the past 24 hours to $2.39 trillion.

It follows U.S. CPI rising 0.4% in October, which is "hotter than expected, even if the headline monthly rate eased to 0.4% from September’s 0.6%," according to CoinShares head of research James Butterfill. "More troubling was the composition," he added. "Food rose 0.5%, services remained firm, and core CPI increased 0.3%, with services excluding rent, a gauge of domestic price pressure the Fed watches closely, rising 0.5%. The inflation problem is therefore no longer easily dismissed as an oil story."

The consumer price index, or CPI, is a way of measuring inflation that tracks the average price changes of everyday goods and services over time. Central banks tend to use CPI to inform whether they'll cut or hike interest rates, meaning higher-than-expected CPI signals a potential Federal Reserve hike.

Polymarket predictors put a 97% chance on the Fed raising interest rates this year, up from 75% at the start of the week. The CME FedWatch tool, meanwhile, sees an 88% chance of a 25 basis point hike, with 12% anticipating a 50 basis point rise.

On top of the CPI, Bitcoin's downward move comes following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company, after reports of multiple affairs including with a suspected Chinese spy and a senior company executive spread.

Huang's departure has sparked "severe volatility across tech stocks, further dampening market risk appetite," Sun told Decrypt. "This has prompted broader portfolio de-risking, amplifying the downward pressure on Bitcoin," he added.

For a crypto rebound to happen, Sun said that Bitcoin needs "long-term allocation capital" to flow back into crypto after ETFs, stablecoins, and digital asset treasury companies have taken a hit in recent weeks.

#4934. Could Your GLP-1s Make You Blind? Here’s What to Make of the FDA’s Latest Notice.

For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is doing something about it.

The FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication. NAION is a rare condition that can lead to vision loss in one eye, and it can be permanent.

Again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION. But it is the first time the FDA has issued a warning about it.

Given that up to 11 percent of Americans currently take a GLP-1 for weight loss, this news stands to impact a lot of people. How concerned should you be if you're one of them? Eye experts and a doctor who prescribes GLP-1s break it down.

Meet the experts: Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system; Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute; and Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

The FDA's notice is designed to flag the potential risk of NAION to people who use GLP-1s. The FDA also notes that the agency will require all manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to add information about the risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

"Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss, with GLP-1 RA use," the notice reads.

The agency cited a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology as well as its own meta-analyses and retrospective cohort study in the notice. They also noted that “NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products.”

However, the complication remains rare: incidents from the FDA’s meta-analysis were just 6.4 events per 100,000 per year for patients using the medications.

The warning is just that—a warning to patients and physicians that this could happen, explains Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. "Most outcome-related issues in medicine should be thought of as being probabilistic—there is a certain chance that events can occur," he says. "This warning indicates that the FDA has reason to believe, at least at this time, that the probability of NAION occurring is higher in patients who take GLP-1 RA drugs."

But Dr. Rizzo stresses that there's no evidence that these drugs cause NAION—just that there's a link.

So…why issue a warning if it's not proven that GLP-1s cause NAION and it's so rare? "The severity of a complication matters alongside its frequency," says Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute. "Even a rare risk deserves attention when it can permanently affect vision." The warning is likely designed to give healthcare providers a heads-up that it could be NAION if a patient has symptoms, he explains.

"It's their duty to report any adverse effects, just so people are aware of them," says Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

While NAION is scary, doctors say it's important to put the data in perspective. "It's extremely rare, but it can happen," Dr. Ali says. Given how much GLP-1s can help with blood sugar management, weight loss, and downstream health effects, Dr. Ali says that the risk of NAION is "not a reason not to seek these medications."

Dr. Rizzo agrees. "I essentially never discourage the general use of GLP-1 RA drugs," he says. "Ultimately, the risk-to-benefit assessment must be decided by the patient, but physicians should provide sufficient information to the patients to better inform their decisions."

People should stay aware of the risk without panicking, Dr. Youssefzadeh says. "It's also worth remembering that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs—people with diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea—already carry a higher baseline risk for NAION, so the risk isn't starting from zero," he adds.

#4933. Nvidia Employees Push Board to Bring Back Jensen Huang: Report

Nvidia Employees Push Board to Bring Back Jensen Huang: Report

Some Nvidia employees are calling on the company's board to bring back Jensen Huang, days after he resigned as CEO following reports of extramarital relationships, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired.

An internal "suggestion box" post, submitted by a longtime engineer prior to Huang's resignation, urged the board to take employee sentiment into account before acting, Wired reported. It has since drawn more than 1,600 comments, several of which asked the board to find a way to reinstate Huang. "If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss," one anonymous commenter wrote.

The post also called on the board to share the findings of its investigation with staff and to formally seek their views on Huang continuing as CEO. One employee went further, sending a companywide email demanding transparency about Huang's exit and declaring: "I stand by Jensen."

In the hours following Huang's departure, some two dozen Nvidia employees posted supportive messages on LinkedIn, while Wired said it could not find any employee posts backing his departure. The engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment, and Nvidia and its new board chair, Harvey Jones, did not immediately respond to the outlet.

Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and a board member on Thursday, ending a 33-year tenure at the company he co-founded. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, and Jones, a former CEO of Synopsys, became the board's first chair. Nvidia did not give a reason for the resignation.

Huang told staff on Sunday that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, without naming anyone.

The New York Times had reported in October that surveillance of Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, indicated that she had developed a "close relationship" with the Nvidia CEO. Per the Times, U.S. officials concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset, while the Financial Times reported that a U.S. memo said the two had been romantically involved. China has denied that she is a spy.

Alice Huang was CEO and chair of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, and was investigated by Singapore police over possible false declarations relating to the company's server purchases, the country's Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday. She was not investigated for espionage, it said.

Police found insufficient evidence that she had committed any offenses, but concluded she had knowingly given them inaccurate information to downplay her role at Megaspeed, according to the ministry. She was issued a stern warning, left Singapore in February and was barred from returning. Investigations into Megaspeed and six other people are ongoing.

Alice Huang is now living in Beijing with the knowledge of security officials, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Justice Department had not yet concluded whether Huang was a spy, and that the FBI was investigating the reports, according to Reuters, which was unable to reach her for comment.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that Jensen Huang had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reported directly to him. Powell has not commented.

On Thursday, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second Nvidia employee, whom it did not name. Nvidia declined to comment to Reuters, and Huang and a representative for the board did not respond. Huang has not commented on the reports since his Sunday email, according to Wired.

The calls inside Nvidia echo criticism of the board's decision from tech and crypto figures. Binance co-founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao called it a mistake for Nvidia to let Huang resign, while Elon Musk said hiring him would be "an honor."

Huang still faces scrutiny in Washington. Congressional committees have asked him to sit for a closed-door interview on December 1 and to testify at a Senate hearing on December 3, as lawmakers examine Nvidia's chip exports to China.

He and Nvidia also face a proposed shareholder class action over his alleged ties to Alice Huang.

Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first under Kress.

#4932. Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low

Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump.

Crypto exchange Gemini has just reported its lowest quarterly retail trading volume in three years, despite an increase in overall crypto trading volume.

Total spot trading volume rose 18% from the second quarter to $4.5 billion, according to Gemini’s Q3 earnings report. Institutional volume climbed 26% to $3.9 billion, while retail volume fell 14% to $600 million, its lowest level since the third quarter of 2023.

Gemini said the quarterly increase in spot trading volume was “supported by increased institutional Zcash activity and expanded affiliated market-making,” but did not give a specific reason for the decline in retail trading.

Despite the retail slump, Gemini’s exchange revenue increased 7% from the previous quarter to $13.4 million as institutional revenue more than doubled. Retail traders remained its largest source of exchange revenue, contributing nearly three-quarters of the total.

A number of crypto exchanges also reported softer crypto trading activity in the most recent quarter.

Coinbase reported softer retail and institutional activity, with consumer spot trading volume falling 9% from the previous quarter to $23.4 billion. Coinbase chief financial officer Alesia Haas said “continued growth in prediction markets helped offset softer crypto trading activity.”

At Robinhood, crypto revenue fell 55% year-on-year to $120 million, offset by a sixfold increase in event-contract revenue to $173 million.

Related: Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off

Gemini also got some help from its own prediction exchange, Gemini Predictions, with revenue from that business unit increasing 52% quarter-on-quarter to $796,000, though it wasn’t significant enough to offset declines elsewhere.

Gemini reported stronger prediction-market activity heading into the fourth quarter, with average daily traders in October running about 50% above the third-quarter average.

Nearly a third of new prediction traders were new to Gemini, more than double the proportion in Q3.

The company is also seeking to distribute its event contracts through other platforms. An August nonbinding agreement with Apex Fintech Solutions would make Gemini Titan the exclusive venue for crypto event contracts distributed through Apex’s futures brokerage to its brokerage customers, subject to definitive agreements.

Gemini is set to host a Q3 earnings call on Friday.

#4929. The Surprising Staying Power of Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy

A24’s Club Kid makes the case for the comedy’s unlikely legacy—and social relevance—in 2026.

EARLY ON IN Jordan Firstman’s dramedy Club Kid, druggie-with-a-heart-of-gold Peter has to shepherd his surprise 10-year-old son through an apartment party. Despite knowing each other for just a few hours, the club promoter and his child hold hands as he guides the way through the bacchanal. It’s a metaphor—what isn’t these days?—and it’s also kind of a recreation of a key sequence in Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy.

In that movie, 5-year-old Julian “Frankenstein” McGrath (played by young Dylan and Cole Sprouse) holds his hand aloft before he steps off the sidewalk, looking for help from his newfound father.

Replace McDonald’s breakfasts with coke and ketamine (plus a Charlie Kirk reference), and A24’s Club Kid is the clear heir apparent to the 1999 Sandler comedy. I’m far from the first person to make the connection. IndieWire’s David Ehrlich’s first-impression response was to ask: “What if A24 made a gay Big Daddy?”

It may seem like an odd movie for a brand like A24 to mirror. However, Big Daddy is somehow the film from the peak Sandler run that has had the longest shelf life. In fact, it may be the late ’90s–early 2000s comedy with the best depiction of the 2026 way of life. For better—or for worse.

Despite the fact that it was a hit at the box office, Big Daddy was reviled at the time of its release, even winning Sandler a Razzie Award for Worst Actor.

And, sure, it’s not the most elegant film—with its near-incessant Hooters jabs and Rob Schneider’s catastrophic accent—but still, it’s managed to stick around in the public consciousness for nearly 30 years. And it’s not just Ehrlich and I who think so.

“I particularly loved Big Daddy. That was my number one,” Paul Thomas Anderson said on an episode of The Bill Simmons Podcast in 2017 when asked about casting Sandler in his film Punch-Drunk Love. “It was a little bit more polished; it was able to be sincere and [mix in] the crazy fucking dirty shit that Sandler likes to do and got the mix really right.”

In Club Kid, promoter Peter (Firstman, who wrote, directed, and stars) somehow ends up in charge of a precocious kid while flailing in both romance and his career. Peter, like Sonny, has to instantly shift his lifestyle, one that only functions when you have little to care for, including yourself. Both protagonists need an act of God to abandon their early-30s doldrums.

And honestly, it’s a sentiment that a lot of people my age (including myself) can relate to.

At the tail end of October, The New York Times published a story (which, thankfully, my parents haven’t sent to me yet) titled “Can’t Afford a Home. Can’t Afford a Baby. Can’t Afford Life. This Is 30.” The gist is that millennials feel burned out now that they know they’re unlikely to achieve the luxuries earlier generations enjoyed.

“In the past, the idea was that you would check all these boxes by 30, give or take. But the more I think about it, so much of that is incredibly out of reach,” says one source in the article. Even decades ago, Sonny Koufax would have probably agreed with the article, before ripping out part of the newspaper to clean up some spilled milk next to his third bowl of cereal of the day. Both films find the hearts at the center of their respective protagonists’ messy, work-in-progress stories. Is there anything more 2026 than that?

When you watch Big Daddy in 2026, you almost forget how much of a schmuck—but vulnerable too—Sandler allowed Sonny to be. I was pleasantly surprised that Sandler ultimately loses his chance at raising Julian by himself. It’s a small, complicated victory for a movie that uses a schlocky, heartfelt monologue about fathers to reach a contrived moral coda, but we’ll take our wins where we can get them.

Greg is a freelance writer and AMC Stubs A-List member when he’s not the Senior Digital Producer at Golf Digest. You can read his movie reviews and existential crises on his Aerial Shot newsletter. He’s sorry in advance if you liked something that he didn’t.

#4924. What “Food Is Medicine” Actually Means, According to a Cardiologist

Plus, Chef Marcus Samuelsson shares easy ways to sneak more plant-based foods into your diet.

Despite what fitfluencers and gym bros might have you believe, eating healthy is about a lot more than counting macros and calories. Every day, scientists are learning more about how our eating habits can influence health beyond just our weight, including blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and risk of developing heart disease.

That's part of the idea behind a buzzy approach to health care known as “food is medicine,” which contends that what we put on our plates can be a meaningful part of preventing and managing disease.

The challenge is understanding what actually helps and turning that knowledge into meals we want to keep eating. To unpack this, Future You host and editorial director of Men’s and Women’s Health Rich Dorment sits down with Marcus Samuelsson, the acclaimed restaurateur and author of the new cookbook, Back to Green, and Louai Razzouk, MD, a cardiologist at NYU Langone Health.

Here’s a look at some of the themes covered in the episode:

Samuelsson says that beso is an Ethiopian drink that combines roasted barley with water or milk of your choice. “You just shake it and this is the best protein shake you can have,” he says. You can find the more specific recipe in Back to Green.

He grew up eating foods like beso as well as shiro, a stew made from chickpea flour, and other Ethiopian “superfoods” that he incorporates into his dishes today.

Dr. Razzouk says it doesn't mean that you can treat a disease with food alone. “It does mean that you may be able to prevent it by having a healthier and more balanced diet, and possibly minimize how many medications you need to be on,” he says.

Dr. Razzouk says that while you may still need to be on medication, food can make a “huge” impact when it comes to managing conditions like diabetes or high cholesterol. “Food impacts our level of inflammation, our insulin sensitivity, our weight,” and our blood pressure, he says.

The first warning sign that a patient’s diet may be less than ideal is if they get most of their food from Uber Eats or another delivery service. “Most of the stuff that we order in, especially living in New York City, contains a lot of saturated fats, a lot of added salt, and a lot of processed food,” he says. He discusses a couple more red flags in the episode, including meal timing.

In his early 20s, traveling in Southeast Asia and Singapore opened his eyes to a new way of eating—and the idea that there’s great food to be found all over the world.

A plant-forward diet doesn't have to exclude animal protein, he says, pointing to the Mediterranean and DASH diets as examples of eating plans that incorporate some meat. “What I tell patients is that typically if you have a choice between getting a source of protein from an animal source versus from plants, then I would try to get it from plants,” he says.

“What I tell patients is that I want you to enjoy your life,” Dr. Razzouk says, adding that fad diets typically don’t work. “What we would like you to do is find a balance,” he says, eating in a way that's enjoyable and that benefits your health.

It's a lentil salad with a coconut turmeric vinaigrette—and Samuelsson breaks down why the flavors work so well together, plus ingredients you may have in the fridge or pantry that can level it up even further.

He’ll often bring home new ingredients (e.g. spirulina) and encourage his son to look up the health benefits before they cook with it together.

Dr. Razzouk says diets high in fiber not only may lower your risk of colon cancer, but they also may lower your level of LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which impact your risk of cardiovascular disease. It also helps keep you full.

Cooking together can be an enjoyable family activity, Samuelsson says. “When I cook waffles and pancakes with my kids, we have fun,” he says. “The kitchen is a mess, but iPads are down, we're spending time together.”

Samuelsson suggests chickpeas, sea moss, and the fruit soursop. Dr. Razzouk suggests nuts (walnuts in particular) and extra-virgin olive oil.

Caitlin is a health and fitness journalist based in New York City. She writes for publications including The Wall Street Journal and Runner’s World. She's completed 12 marathons, including the six World Marathon Majors, is semi-fluent in French, and volunteers as a greeter on The High Line. Follow her on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#4922. ‘Roadmap is Complete,' Cardano Founder Charles Hoskinson Says

‘Roadmap is Complete,' Cardano Founder Charles Hoskinson Says

Charles Hoskinson said that the Cardano "roadmap is complete" and that everything he said would be built has finished. It came during a YouTube livestream Saturday where Hoskinson sparred with disgruntled investors as ADA sits down 94% from its 2021 high, per Decrypt data.

One viewer, named shevilkid1738, pushed Hoskinson's buttons by claiming he'd promised Cardano would overtake Bitcoin. The Cardano founder clapped back, saying there was no evidence he ever said that.

"I never promised that. I said I'd love for it to happen, and I believe that Cardano is a better store of value than Bitcoin is for a variety of reasons," Hoskinson said. "I don't promise price appreciation, or people overturning things. I say it's absolutely possible."

Shevilkid1738 responded over an hour later with a quote where Hoskinson said he "thinks" Cardano is "probably" going to become the biggest cryptocurrency in the world. Hoskinson highlighted the word think and said that he has "taken it as far as I can," explaining that the network is now decentralized and doesn't rely on him as a founder.

The viewer wasn't happy and called it "insane" for a founder to no longer have a responsibility to those who invested in their project.

"Under what conditions does that obligation end?" Hoskinson said, "The roadmap is complete. Everything I said is going to be built has been built. It reached four times the value of Honda. There's millions of people that have used it, and millions of people continue to use it. It is self-determining and self-governing, with its ability to pick and choose its own leaders without my consent."

Cardano’s roadmap was split into five eras: Byron, Shelly, Goguen, Basho, and Voltaire.

Byron launched the network in September 2017, Shelley added staking in July 2020, and Goguen brought smart contracts via the Alonzo hard fork in September 2021. Basho, the scaling era, came via the Vasil upgrade in September 2022, before the Chang hard fork kicked off Voltaire, the governance era, in September 2024.

The final piece to the puzzle occurred in January 2025, when the Plomin hard fork gave ADA holders "real voting power" over the blockchain’s future. This marked the transition to "full decentralized governance," and apparently the end of the final roadmap era.

"The goal was simple. There's a roadmap. Byron, Basho, Shelley, et cetera, et cetera, and it's done," Hoskinson said. "I have no power over this ecosystem."

Ultimately, though, Hoskinson says the issue that investors have is financial.

"You want me to pump your bags. That's what you're really saying. The job's not done till it's pumped," he said. "But guess what? It's never done then, because somebody comes in at $3 ADA, and then expects it to be five. And then somebody comes in at $5 ADA and expects it to be seven. If you retire at five, you've defrauded the person at five. If you retire at three, you've defrauded the person at three. There's no winning."

ADA hit an all-time high of $3.09 in 2021 and has been on a downward slide ever since. By 2023, it hit a low of $0.25 before pumping 384% to a high of $1.21 by the end of 2024. Since then, its price has tanked 86% to $0.17.

"Apparently, I have to go pump your bags, and if I don't, I'm a scammer," Hoskinson said. "Would you sign up for that deal? Would any human being sign up for that? I thought slavery was made illegal."

#4920. Trump nominates Hester Peirce successor among SEC, CFTC picks

The White House also named a former CFTC commissioner and two CLARITY Act veterans as nominees to fill vacancies at the SEC and CFTC.

US President Donald Trump has nominated Steven Levine to replace former Securities and Exchange Commission Commissioner Hester Peirce, one of the agency’s most prominent crypto advocates, as part of four nominations to fill vacancies at the SEC and Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The White House’s latest announcement on Thursday named two nominees each for the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, agencies whose decisions help shape US cryptocurrency regulation, among other functions. All four nominations require Senate confirmation.

The nominations would replenish several commissioner roles. The SEC currently has only two of its five commissioner seats filled, while CFTC Chairman Michael Selig is the sole member of his agency’s five-seat commission.

The nominations come weeks before Democrats are set to take control of the Senate in January, giving a narrow window for Republicans to confirm Trump’s picks.

Related: House Finance panel chair says regulator actions on crypto ‘fall short’ of CLARITY bill

Levine, a Republican, was nominated for an SEC term ending June 5, 2030, replacing Peirce, who left the agency in October. Peirce was a leading advocate for clearer crypto rules at the SEC, helping shape its approach to digital assets as the former head of its Crypto Task Force, while Levine’s views on crypto regulation are less publicly established.

Trump also nominated Democrat Kristin Johnson, a former CFTC commissioner, for the SEC seat held by Caroline Crenshaw, whose term has also expired. Johnson’s proposed term ends June 5, 2029. Johnson has advocated for stronger customer protections and conflict-of-interest rules for crypto firms in her time at the CFTC.

For the CFTC, Trump nominated Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland, both of whom worked on the Clarity Act. CFTC Chairman Mike Selig called them “two strong bipartisan picks” for CFTC commissioners and said he looked forward to working with them upon their confirmation.

The nominees would typically appear before the Senate Banking Committee for the SEC positions and the Senate Agriculture Committee for the CFTC roles. Following committee consideration, their nominations would go to the full Senate, where confirmation requires a majority vote.

#4918. Functional Core Workouts Are the Key to Moving Better in and Out of the Gym

Add these 15 expert-approved exercises into your weekly routine.

I don’t know about you, but doing core exercises is my least favorite part of workouts. Unfortunately, though, neglecting functional core training can make a big difference in your total-body strength, and how you move day to day.

Functional training focuses on compound movements that engage multiple muscle groups simultaneously and mimic the way our bodies move during everyday activities. Functionally training the core, specifically, involves strengthening the abdominal muscles that attach to the pelvis or spine.

For instance, a farmer’s carry mirrors the movement of carrying grocery bags. “This is an example of ‘bracing and carrying,’ where you need to keep a tight, braced core to carry the heavy weight,” says Corrine Carnation, CPT, a personal and group trainer at Equinox and creator of the Better You, Better Living program. Plus, a weak core can lead to poor posture and an increased risk of injury.

But the benefits extend way beyond preparing your body for real-life activities and protecting against pain or injury—keep reading for all the reasons you should do functional core movements.

Meet the experts: Corrine Carnation, CPT, is a personal and group trainer at Equinox. Cori Ritchey, CSCS, is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and conditioning coach and group fitness instructor in New York City.

Time: 30 minutes | Equipment (optional): kettlebell, dumbbells, slam ball, resistance band, or Pilates ring | Good for: core, hips, back

Instructions: Choose 5 to 6 exercises from the list below. Complete 2 to 3 sets of the indicated number of reps for each move. Aim to integrate functional core exercises into your training routine once or twice a week.

As these exercises become easier with practice, challenge yourself by increasing resistance while slightly decreasing the number of reps. For example, if 3 sets of 10 reps using bodyweight alone feels easy, try adding a weight or resistance band for 2 or 3 sets of 8 reps. By the last rep of each set, you should feel ready to stop but not completely at failure. When in doubt, start with bodyweight only, then add resistance until you feel the exercise is challenging, but doable.

Pro tip: Exercises aren’t one-size-fits-all, so it’s important to recognize when an exercise is either too challenging, too easy, or not comfortable for you. Keep in mind that every exercise can be modified if needed!

Why it rocks: The suitcase carry prepares the core for real-life activities such as carrying heavy things by your sides. It strengthens the core by making you resist the urge to bend, improving stability and balance—the added grip demand is a fun challenge, too.

1. Holding a weight in one hand, stand up tall and pull your shoulders back and down to prevent them from rolling forward. Keep your core tight and spine neutral.

2. Walk forward for 30 to 60 seconds while maintaining a strong grip and upright posture.

4. Turn around and pick the weight up again, this time with your left hand. Complete 4 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: The halo exercise improves shoulder mobility and stability while strengthening your core. Moving the weight around your head causes a perturbation (or distracting force) to your body, forcing you to stabilize using your core. This particular halo variation has the added benefit of enhancing upper-body strength, targeting the shoulders, back, and arms.

1. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding one dumbbell in front of your chest with both hands and elbows bent at 90 degrees.

2. Slowly circle the dumbbell around your head, moving it clockwise from ear to ear, elbows hugging in.

3. Return to start and repeat the movement counterclockwise. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: Have you ever worried about straining your back when picking something up or twisting? This move strengthens the core, improves stability, and builds rotational strength to protect your body during these movements.

1. Sit on the floor with your knees bent and upper body leaned back until abs are engaged (aim for a 45-degree angle relative to the floor). Hold a slam ball or dumbbell close to your chest with your elbows bent.

2. Keeping your arms slightly bent, twist your torso to the left and slam the ball on the floor next to your left hip.

3. Twist your torso through center to the right and slam the ball on the floor near your right hip. That's 1 rep.

4. Continue alternating for a total of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: The overhead slam exercise requires you to stabilize your body as you lift and forcefully throw the ball down to the floor. It also strengthens your shoulders, arms, and upper back while improving explosive power and coordination.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, a soft bend in knees, and core engaged, while holding a slam ball at your chest with both hands.

2. Rise up tall on your toes and extend your arms overhead holding the slam ball.

3. Bend at your hips (hinging forward slightly) and slam the ball on the floor directly in front of you. Exhale as you throw the ball down toward the floor with force. Be careful not to arch your back.

4. Catch the ball on the bounce while lowering back into the squat position. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: The wood chop exercise helps strengthen your core by working your abs and obliques, which can boost your twisting power and stability, building strength and coordination.

1. Start in a half-kneeling position with your left leg forward and your right leg back, both bent at 90 degrees, holding a dumbbell in front of your chest.

2. With your arms straight, torso upright, and hips facing forward, swiftly lower the weight diagonally across your body to the right hip while twisting to the right. Then, raise the weight to upper left diagonal while twisting to the left. That's 1 rep.

3. Complete 10 reps, then repeat on the other side.

Why it rocks: Keeping your lower back and head flush with the floor while your limbs shift weight will engage your deep core stabilizers. Being able to lift your legs and arms from this position is essential for a healthy spine.

1. Lie faceup holding one dumbbell horizontally in front of your chest with both hands. Lift legs to a tabletop position with your knees over hips, your lower back glued to the floor, and your core engaged.

2. Keeping one leg at a 90-degree angle, lower the other to tap your heel to the floor. As your leg lowers, reach your arms above your head to lower the weight toward the floor behind your head.

3. Engage your core to lift both your arms and leg back to start, then repeat on the opposite side. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise recruits your abdominal muscles to maintain balance and stability. A resistance band offers an added challenge for the core and lower body.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and your hands on your hips or relaxed at your sides. (Optional: Place a resistance band around the arches of both feet.)

2. Balancing on one leg, draw one knee up toward your chest, hold for 1 second, then return it to the floor.

3. Repeat on the opposite side, alternating for 30 seconds. That’s 1 rep.

Why it rocks: Planks help you build the strength to push yourself up from the floor, which is important for many day-to-day activities. Adding the knee drive challenges your upper body and core to stabilize, improving your balance and coordination with uneven movements.

1. Start in a high plank position with your right foot lifted slightly up off the floor.

2. Exhale and pull your right knee toward your chest while rounding the spine to bring your nose toward your knee.

3. With control, reverse movement to return to plank position with right foot lifted. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise challenges you to sit up and lie down without using your hands, which requires strong core muscles. You can do it with a Pilates ring, a ball, or no equipment at all.

1. Lie faceup with your legs slightly bent, heels on floor, and arms extended straight above your head. (Optional: Place a mini resistance band around your wrists for an added challenge.)

2. Engage your core and draw your belly button in as you slowly begin to curl your spine off the mat one vertebra at a time. Roll up to an upright seated position while keeping biceps by the ears and arms reaching to the ceiling.

3. Once you reach the upright position, gradually reverse the movement by slowly rolling back down to the lying position. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise targets the glutes and core, the muscles needed to lift your hips. It's great for anyone who sits a lot, as it both strengthens and mobilizes the hips.

1. Lie faceup with knees bent and feet planted shoulder-width apart on the floor. Place your arms on the floor by your sides or for an added challenge, extend arms above with your hands directly above your shoulders and your palms facing in.

2. Engage your core as you press up into a glute bridge with your knees, hips, and shoulders in alignment, and hold this position.

3. From here, raise your right leg to a 90-degree angle, keeping the stationary leg firmly on the floor and pelvis stable. Return right foot to meet left foot in starting position. That’s 1 rep.

4. Continue alternating legs with your butt lifted and complete 10 to 12 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: The classic side plank targets the obliques, which are essential for stability and rotation in daily activities. It also works your shoulders and hips, promoting good posture and alignment.

1. Lie on your right side with your legs bent, your right elbow directly under your shoulder, and your left hand palm down.

2. Lift your hips off the mat, extending your legs to form a straight line from your head to heels.

3. Hold the position for 30 seconds, then repeat on the opposite side. That’s 1 rep.

Why it rocks: It's similar to the suitcase carry, but levels up the move a bit by testing your stabilization, as you have to stay upright even though the weight is trying to pull you down. Plus, it boosts your grip strength.

1. Stand up straight with feet shoulder-width apart and dumbbell in left hand.

2. Extend your right arm out to the side at a 45-degree angle from your body.

3. Slowly lift your left leg up until knee is at hip height.

4. Then, with control, lower your leg down to the floor. Repeat with right leg. That's 1 rep.

5. Complete 10 to 12 reps, then switch the dumbbell to your right hand.

Why it rocks: It targets your obliques, but also challenges your other core muscles in a more uncommon position. Additionally, it works your spinal mobility.

1. Kneel on left knee with toes pointed to the right, and right foot planted firmly to the side of body, holding a kettlebell in right hand.

2. Rack the kettlebell at chest, then lift it overhead, keeping eyes on the weight.

3. Slowly lower body down until left hand reaches the floor, then continue lowering until elbow and forearm reach the floor.

4. Reverse the movement with control and return to start. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: It's important to train rotation because we're constantly rotating in real life. Plank hip dips strengthen the obliques and stabilize the spine.

1. Start in a forearm plank position with elbows under shoulders and knees, hips, and torso in a straight line.

2. Drop right hip toward the floor, then return to center.

3. Immediately drop the left hip toward the floor.

Why it rocks: This move is one of the best for training functional power, and it demands stabilization from your core.

1. Stand with feet slightly wider than hip-width apart. Hold a kettlebell in front of your body with both hands, arms straight.

2. With a slight bend in the knees and a flat back, hinge at the hips and swing the kettlebell back through the legs. Use that momentum to stand and swing the kettlebell out in front of your body, up to shoulder height.

3. Thrust the hips forward and engage the glutes and core as you stand up straight. When the kettlebell hits shoulder height, the knees should be straight and glutes contracted in a full hip extension.

4. Allow the kettlebell to swing back down through the legs, while hinging at the hips. That's 1 rep.

The best functional core workouts include bodyweight and resistance exercises that challenge the core in different positions and directions. Your core is not one-dimensional, so it’s important to strengthen your body through movements that involve twisting, bending, and stabilizing in all directions. For example, a traditional situp only engages the core in a single plane of motion, but a workout with a Russian twist (for rotational movement), lateral side bends (for side-to-side movement), and plank variations (for multidirectional stability) ensures you are hitting your core muscles from all angles.

Carnation notes the importance of first activating your core before jumping right into a workout. To do so, she recommends the following: “Act as if someone is about to throw a basketball at your stomach.” It might sound odd, but this cue can be really effective in helping you tighten and brace your core to get ready for impact. It’s best to practice this abdominal bracing technique before going into more advanced exercises in order to ensure your core is engaged and ready for action, Carnation says.

#4917. Bitcoin slides below $70K amid thin liquidity, ETF outflows

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 as crypto sentiment hit its lowest level in more than four months, with analysts warning of institutional outflows, thinning liquidity and elevated leverage.

Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday, extending its recent decline as investor sentiment deteriorated amid institutional outflows, tightening liquidity and broader macroeconomic pressures.

Bitcoin (BTC) is trading at $68,607.23 at the time of writing, down 9.2% in the last week, according to CoinGecko.

The drop coincided with a sharp decline in market sentiment. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index fell to 20 on Friday, its lowest reading in more than four months, putting it in “extreme fear.” The index last reached that level on July 8.

Bitcoin’s seven-day price chart. Source: CoinGecko

Vikram Subburaj, CEO of crypto exchange Giottus, attributed Bitcoin’s weakness to institutional outflows, tightening crypto liquidity and expectations of a December Federal Reserve interest rate hike. “Investors should avoid chasing short-term dips or using excessive leverage,” he said.

In a Friday report, 10x Research highlighted Bitcoin’s divergence from US equities. Between Nov. 5 and Nov. 12, Bitcoin declined 5.9% while the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.4%, suggesting the cryptocurrency was responding more to rising Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar than to technology stocks.

The research firm said Bitcoin was increasingly trading alongside gold, which fell 5.5% over the same period, as the US 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5%.

Meanwhile, institutional trading platform Talos also warned that thin liquidity and elevated leverage could amplify market volatility. Its weekly report showed Bitcoin order-book depth across major exchanges fell to $72 million on Nov. 9, roughly 33% below normal levels.

“Liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction,” said Tanay Ved, senior research associate at Talos. “A rebuild in order-book depth and a turn in capital flows would provide a firmer foundation for recovery.”

The selloff follows sustained withdrawals from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs). BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded more than $2 billion in net outflows across nine consecutive trading sessions through Wednesday, while broader funds shed nearly $1.44 billion over five sessions.

Preliminary Farside Investors data showed another $47.7 million in net outflows on Thursday, although figures for BlackRock and Fidelity were still pending.
